mem.t: For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

lessons.title: The Disciples Who Wanted the Best Seats
lessons.theme: On the road with Jesus, the hardest thing to lay down is the longing for the top seat

v: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came near to him, saying, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we will ask.”
He said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said to him, “Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left hand, in your glory.”
But Jesus said to them, “You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, and to be baptised with the baptism that I am baptised with?”
They said to him, “We are able.” Jesus said to them, “You shall indeed drink the cup that I drink, and you shall be baptised with the baptism that I am baptised with;
but to sit at my right hand and at my left hand is not mine to give, but for whom it has been prepared.”

lessons.still: Before you open your laptop, rest your hands on the desk, palms up. Say to the Lord: “Lord, today I don’t ask to sit next to anyone important. I only ask to walk behind you.” Breathe slowly three times, then begin.
teach: Jesus has just predicted, for the third time, that he will be handed over, mocked and killed, and will rise after three days (Mark 10:33–34). The words have barely left his lips when James and John step forward with a blank cheque: “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we will ask.” What they want is the two seats on either side of him in his glory. Jesus does not explode. He simply says, “You don’t know what you are asking.” Then he asks whether they can drink his cup and share his baptism. The cup and the baptism he means are suffering, and a cross.

At work, many of us quietly draw up a seating plan for the company’s year-end dinner: who sits beside the chairman, who gets the table by the door. Before the promotion list is out, we have already pencilled our name into the box. James and John’s problem was not that they wanted to do good work, but that they wanted to secure their place first. Their eyes were on the seat; Jesus was pointing at the cup.

Gently, Jesus turns his disciples’ gaze from “Where will I sit?” to “What cup can you drink?” That is where a change of mindset begins. The self-centred life asks, “What position can I get?” A follower asks, “What does the Lord want me to carry?” James later became the first apostle to die for Christ, and John suffered for him on the island of Patmos. They did drink that cup, and in it they met their Lord. May he change us, too, from people who jostle for seats into people willing to drink the cup.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-centredness is “I want to be lord and king”, and it shows itself in grabbing for position. Pride is leaving your proper place to seize power. To let Jesus be King is to hand the seating plan back to him and return to the place of a follower.
lessons.scene: Yijun is a financial adviser at a bank, and next month her department will choose a new assistant manager. Her director tells her quietly, “The general manager is hosting dinner on Friday. Go and sit next to him, chat a bit, and the job is yours.” She looks at the booking notice on her phone, her finger hovering over “Confirm attendance”, and something in her feels uneasy.
q: Who is God? — Instead of rebuking them, Jesus answered his disciples with a “cup”. What does that show you about the kind of Lord he is?
Who am I? — On the seating plan in your heart, which box would you most like your name in?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yijun, how would you go to Friday’s dinner — or how would you not go?
lessons.jesus: James and John asked to sit at the Lord’s right and left. In the end, those at Jesus’ right and left were two robbers (Mark 15:27). His “glory” was not a throne but a cross. He gave the places beside him to sinners, so that people like us, who scramble for seats, might be welcomed by him.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you know the seating plan in my heart. I often want to sit a little closer to power and forget to walk behind you. Forgive my self-centredness, and stop me calculating whose side is most useful to be on. Whether I am placed at the top table or by the door today, I am willing to drink the cup you give me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Notice one moment when you angle for position, and give it to the Lord
In a meeting, leave the best seat for a colleague
Write down one unseen task the Lord may be asking you to carry
lessons.noon: “You don’t know what you are asking.” — Lord, right now I give you the seat I want, and ask only to follow you.

lessons.title: Not So Among You
lessons.theme: Kingdom leadership turns the direction of power upside down

v: When the ten heard it, they began to be indignant towards James and John.
Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognised as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so amongst you, but whoever wants to become great amongst you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first amongst you shall be bondservant of all.

lessons.still: Once you are seated, quietly say the names of the people you will lead or work with today. Tell the Lord: “Lord, in your kingdom it is not so. Today let me serve rather than control.”
teach: When the other ten heard what James and John had asked, “they began to be indignant”. They were angry not because the two were too worldly, but because they wanted the same seats. Jesus called them all together and described the leadership of the nations: rulers who “lord it over them”, great ones who “exercise authority over them”. That was Rome’s way: whoever is on top keeps those below pinned down. Then he spoke words that turned history over: “But it shall not be so amongst you.” Whoever wants to be great must be a servant; whoever wants to be first must be the bondservant of all.

The most important part of an office tower is often not the chairman’s suite on the top floor but the plant room in the basement. Water, power, air conditioning, the network, fire safety — all depend on rooms no visitor ever tours. If the plant room fails, the whole building stops. Kingdom leadership is like that: not seen at the top, but holding everyone up from the bottom. Real authority is the power that lets other people do their work well.

Jesus did not say, “Don’t be great.” He said, “Whoever wants to become great amongst you shall be your servant.” He did not abolish leadership; he redefined it. Proud leadership provokes pride — the ten disciples’ anger proves it. Humble leadership draws out humility, so a team no longer needs to watch its back. Change from the inside out starts with the mindset: my position is not a platform for others to serve me, but a post from which I serve them.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When Jesus is King, I am no longer king. Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. Building God’s order begins with power that flows downwards.
lessons.scene: Guoqiang has just been made site manager for a construction firm. The senior tradesmen, all older than him, nod in meetings and then do as they please, and the schedule keeps slipping. The company has authorised him to issue warnings and dock bonuses. At half past five this morning he stands at the site gate, a stack of warning slips in one hand, his other hand free to help unload the steel.
q: Who is God? — Jesus said, “It shall not be so amongst you.” What does that reveal about the kingdom in his heart?
Who am I? — Are you more like the ruler who lords it over others, or like the plant room in the basement?
How shall I respond? — What should Guoqiang pick up first this morning? And what should you pick up first in your team?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not merely teach upside-down leadership; he lived it. He asked, “Who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves?” and then said, “But I am amongst you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). The King of kings chose to stand where the waiters stand, so that we could sit at his banquet.
lessons.pray: Lord, your kingdom is not like this, but I often am: wanting to control, to be obeyed, to win. Change the way I see power. Today let me be like the plant room, quietly holding my colleagues up. Give me wisdom not to relax what must be held firm, and not to refuse the service that is needed. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Ask one team member, “How can I help you do this well?”
Today, make a request instead of pulling rank
Take on one chore that no one else wants
lessons.noon: “But it shall not be so amongst you” — Lord, right now let me serve rather than control.

lessons.title: Jesus’ Job Description
lessons.theme: The Son of Man came to serve, and that rewrites why I go to work

v: For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater amongst you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.
For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am amongst you as one who serves.

lessons.still: On your commute, close your eyes for ten seconds and say: “Lord, you did not come to be served. Today I don’t go to work to be served either, but to serve.”
teach: The title “Son of Man” comes from Daniel. That figure comes with the clouds of heaven, and “dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him” (Daniel 7:14). By rights, the Son of Man is the one in all creation most entitled to be served. Yet Jesus says, “For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” The one who most deserves service became the most complete servant — and more than that, he gave his life to pay the price of our release.

Every role comes with a job description: duties, targets, reporting lines. Jesus’ job description is very short — just two lines. Line one: serve people. Line two: give your life as a ransom. Nothing about building a personal brand or climbing a grade. Our job description may list sales figures, projects and deadlines, but on the back of that page the Lord has added a line: use this job to serve people.

Change your mindset and you change your life. If I go to work only to be affirmed, looked after and valued, every day will feel like not enough. If I go to work to serve, even an email or a phone call carries meaning. This is the 920 practice: every colleague, client and supplier connected to me is one of my “2”, someone in relationship with me. I am not merely their manager or competitor; I am someone the Lord has sent to serve them.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example — he came to serve. 920 reminds me that everyone connected to me is my “2”; as I practise the self-emptied “0” life in serving them, the Spirit’s fruit will grow.
lessons.scene: Priya is a senior consultant with an IT consultancy in Singapore. At six in the evening the client’s admin assistant calls again with a small question outside the contract scope — five minutes would fix it. Her teammates say, “Tell her to raise a ticket, or it’ll never end.” Priya’s finger is already on the “Transfer to ticketing” button.
q: Who is God? — The Son of Man should be served by all nations, yet he came to serve. How does that help you know Jesus?
Who am I? — If you wrote your real motive for going to work as a job description, what would line one say?
How shall I respond? — How should Priya decide between serving and keeping sensible boundaries? What will you do today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ service went all the way to the cross. He washed feet, healed the sick and fed crowds, and in the end he gave his own life as a ransom. “To serve, and to give his life” — his service was not a management technique but sacrifice that loved to the end. We can serve because he served us first.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you did not come to be served but to serve me, even to give your life for me. Rewrite the job description in my heart, so that my first reason for going to work is to serve. With every call and every request today, remind me that you have sent me there, and give me wisdom about boundaries. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Stick a note by your screen: “Today I came to serve”
Reply promptly to one request you meant to put off
Pray for one client or colleague for a minute
lessons.noon: “But I am amongst you as one who serves.” — Lord, right now let me serve someone in my next task.

lessons.title: The Lord Who Took a Towel
lessons.theme: Servant leadership is not weakness; it is knowing who you are and kneeling willingly

v: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.

lessons.still: Stand up and lay your jacket or ID badge over the back of your chair. Pause for five seconds. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you know who I am and whose I am. Today I don’t need to prove myself. I am free to serve.”
teach: John’s account is careful: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God, arose from supper.” Notice the link. Precisely because he knew his authority, his origin and his destiny, he laid aside his outer garments, wrapped a towel around his waist, poured water into a basin and washed his disciples’ feet one by one. Foot-washing was the lowest servant’s job. Jesus did it, and lost nothing of his lordship.

A head chef who is truly good at her craft is not afraid to roll up her sleeves after closing and scrub pans alongside the apprentices. She knows her knife skills and her reputation will not vanish at the sink. It is the insecure who are most afraid of doing things “beneath them”. The strength of servant leadership comes from a settled identity, not from how others see you.

Servant leadership is not people-pleasing, nor is it a life without boundaries. After washing their feet, Jesus sat down and said, “You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.” He served, and he was still Lord; he knelt, and he still taught, corrected and led. The self-emptied life is not having no self; it is no longer being bound by self, and so entering and living out the boundless. Those who know who they are in Christ are free to pick up the towel.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to your proper place — letting people be people and God be God. The self-emptied life is not emptiness but entry into the boundless; denying self is a choice made with authority, not a powerless retreat.
lessons.scene: Bohan is CEO of a thirty-person start-up. Last night the system went down for four hours because of one engineer’s mistake. In this morning’s board video call, the directors want to know who is responsible. Bohan stayed up all night with that engineer to fix it. Now the camera light comes on, and it is his turn to speak.
q: Who is God? — Jesus washed feet knowing the Father had given all things into his hands. What kind of Lord does that show you?
Who am I? — What kind of task do you fear is “beneath you”? Is there a fear of losing face or power behind it?
How shall I respond? — How can Bohan take responsibility before the board and still lead the team to improve afterwards?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knelt before his disciples and held their dusty feet in his hands. The text implies that even Judas, who would betray him, was among them (John 13:10–11). All things were in his hands, and he used those hands to wash feet. Later those same hands were nailed to a cross, washing us clean entirely.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you knew the Father had put all things into your hands, and still you picked up a towel. Let me find a settled identity in you, so I don’t need a title to prove myself. Give me courage today to take responsibility, and wisdom to keep the standards that matter. Let my leadership be like yours — with authority, and with a towel. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Do one small task “beneath your grade”, like clearing the meeting table
When the team gets it wrong, start with “I share responsibility”
After serving, kindly and clearly explain the standard going forward
lessons.noon: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” — Lord, right now I am willing to pick up the towel.

lessons.title: Wash a Colleague’s Feet Today
lessons.theme: Service is not a theory; it is one concrete act today

v: For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.
For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.”
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and ask the Holy Spirit to bring one colleague’s face to mind. Tell the Lord: “Lord, today let me wash this colleague’s feet with one small act.” Hold on to that name.
teach: Paul reminds the Galatians that they were called to freedom, but freedom is not an opportunity to indulge the flesh: “through love be servants to one another.” Service is not an optional module. He adds that the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” After washing his disciples’ feet, Jesus said, “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” The blessing is not in knowing but in doing.

Food-delivery apps talk about “the last mile”. However good the meal, if it never reaches the customer’s door, it hasn’t been delivered. Service is the same. We have spent a week on servant leadership and our hearts have been moved, but if love stops at “read”, it is like a meal left on the restaurant’s pickup counter, going cold with no one to eat it. Today, love needs to be delivered into one colleague’s hands.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Service need not be dramatic: refill the paper tray for a swamped colleague, listen for five minutes to someone who has just taken a complaint, look over a newcomer’s report, volunteer for a shift no one wants. These small acts are what the Spirit’s fruit looks like at work — love, kindness, goodness, gentleness. The “2” in 920 is not a concept; it is the person you will meet today.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. 920: choose one “2” today and serve them with a self-emptied “0” heart, so that the Spirit’s “9” fruits can be seen and tasted in your workplace.
lessons.scene: Kelvin is a senior auditor at an accounting firm in Kuala Lumpur. At nine o’clock at night in audit season, he has finally finished his part, and his wife messages to ask when he’ll be home. At the next desk, a new junior is still reconciling a pile of bank statements, has got it wrong twice and has red eyes. Kelvin picks up his bag, then stops.
q: Who is God? — Jesus said, “Blessed are you if you do them.” Where is the blessing he gives actually found?
Who am I? — Are you someone who knows a great deal about serving but often stops at “read”?
How shall I respond? — How can Kelvin care for both his wife and the new junior? Who is your “2” today?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus lit a charcoal fire on the shore of Galilee, cooked fish and bread, and said to disciples who had fished all night and caught nothing, “Come and eat breakfast!” (John 21:12). He did not begin with a review of their failure; he fed them first. The risen Lord still serves the weary with his own hands.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for making breakfast for your tired disciples on the shore. I know so much about serving, yet so often I don’t do it. Today let me see the colleague who needs serving, and give me a little time, a little patience and a little courage to put your love into their hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the name of one colleague you will serve today
Do one concrete thing for them, without needing anyone to know
Before leaving, note what fruit today’s service produced
lessons.noon: “Through love be servants to one another.” — Lord, right now let me deliver your love to one colleague.

mem.t: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.

lessons.title: He Must Increase
lessons.theme: My joy is to let Jesus be in focus while I step into the background

v: John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.
You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full.
He must increase, but I must decrease.

lessons.still: Sit down and turn your phone face down. Say softly: “Lord, you must increase and I must decrease. Today let people see you in me more than they see me.”
teach: John the Baptist’s disciples were anxious: “He who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptises, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26). In their place, we might feel we had lost market share. But John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” He called himself the friend of the bridegroom, who stands by and rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Then he summed up his life in one line: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

Every good photographer understands focus: the subject sharp and clear, the background soft and blurred. The background is not unimportant — it is what makes the subject stand out. John was content to be the background so that Jesus could be the focus. At work we want the lens on us: our name on the last slide, the boss knowing the result was ours. John teaches a different kind of professionalism: adjust the focus onto Jesus, and be glad to be the soft background.

To “decrease” is not to put yourself down or to give up. John kept preaching faithfully and confronting sin courageously, right up to his imprisonment. What decreased was his self-centredness; what increased was the name of Christ. The self-centred life needs to be seen in order to feel valuable. The self-emptied life knows its worth is given from heaven, and so can rejoice sincerely when others flourish. John calls it a joy that is “made full”.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on yourself, others or circumstances. When Jesus receives all the glory, I am freed from comparison and can truly rejoice when others flourish.
lessons.scene: Xiaowen is a senior nurse at a hospital in Taipei. Last year she personally trained a younger nurse who has now been made ward manager. Everyone takes their questions to the new manager, even the patients’ families. At lunch, a few colleagues gather round Xiaowen and whisper, “What makes her so special? You know far more than she does.” They are all waiting for her to answer.
q: Who is God? — John said, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” What kind of God gives everything?
Who am I? — When you see someone flourish more than you, what is your first reaction?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiaowen, how would you answer those colleagues?
lessons.jesus: As soon as John saw Jesus, he said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). His whole work was to point to Jesus. And Jesus himself was willing to “decrease”, coming down from heaven’s glory to a manger and a cross, so that we might flourish in God’s love.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit I badly want to be seen, and I feel a sour twist when others are given more. Adjust my heart like a lens, so that you are sharp and I am soft. If someone is praised more than I am today, give me the joy of the bridegroom’s friend, and let me be truly glad for them. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Sincerely congratulate a colleague who has been recognised
When others complain about someone, add nothing; speak well instead
Do one thing that helps the team succeed without your name on it
lessons.noon: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” — Lord, right now let others see you in me.

lessons.title: Applause That Bites
lessons.theme: Applause is not wrong; pocketing it is deadly

v: On an appointed day, Herod dressed himself in royal clothing, sat on the throne, and gave a speech to them.
The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”
Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.
But the word of God grew and multiplied.
Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.

lessons.still: Breathe deeply. Bring your hands together, then open them as if handing something over. Tell the Lord: “Lord, if any praise comes my way today, I will pass it on to you.”
teach: Herod Agrippa put on his royal robes, sat on the throne and gave a speech. The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” The flattery was absurd enough, but the text names the real problem: “an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory.” He swallowed it whole, taking glory that belongs to God alone. Then Luke adds, almost drily: “But the word of God grew and multiplied.” The mighty king fell; God’s word kept on going.

Corner shops often hold parcels for collection. The staff handle valuable items every day, yet none of them belong to the staff. Their job is to receive, keep safe and hand over to the rightful recipient; opening a parcel and keeping it would be theft. Applause at work is a parcel held for collection: the sales figures, the award, the client’s thank-you letter pass through our hands, but they have a true addressee. Pride is treating the held parcel as our own.

“Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” Herod’s end reminds us that pride is no small flaw; it is the root of the fall — wanting to replace God. God is not a jealous boss; he knows glory is too heavy for us to carry. Giving God the glory is not false modesty but returning to our proper place: letting God be God and people be people. Then we can enjoy being affirmed without being crushed by it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. Self-centredness is wanting to replace God, and it shows itself as pride. Passing the glory on to God is returning to our proper place, and it builds God’s order in the workplace.
lessons.scene: Deming manages an electronics factory in Shenzhen. This year the yield rate rose sharply — in fact the result of three months of late nights by the quality-control team reworking the process. At the year-end assembly, the group chairman announces, “Deming is our hero! Deming, tell us how you did it.” Applause fills the hall, and the microphone is passed to Deming.
q: Who is God? — Herod fell, but God’s word grew and multiplied. What does that show you about how God regards his glory?
Who am I? — Is there a “held parcel” you have quietly kept for yourself recently?
How shall I respond? — What could Deming’s first sentence be when he takes the microphone?
lessons.jesus: When the crowds were about to take Jesus by force to make him king, he “withdrew again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). He said, “I don’t receive glory from men” (John 5:41). The one who truly deserves all glory did not crave human applause; his whole heart was set on glorifying the Father.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for the results you have given in my work. I confess that when the applause starts, I easily take it as my own. Keep me from becoming a Herod, and teach me, like Jesus, not to receive glory from people. Today I will pass every compliment on to you, and remember the colleagues who worked behind the scenes. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When praised, name a colleague who worked on it with you
Pray silently: “This glory belongs to you, Lord”
Send a thank-you message to someone who helped behind the scenes
lessons.noon: “But the word of God grew and multiplied.” — Lord, right now I pass the applause on to you.

lessons.title: Trace the Source of Praise
lessons.theme: When you are affirmed, follow the grace back and give the glory to God

v: For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?
Not to us, LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake.

lessons.still: Open your hands and look at them. Tell the Lord: “Lord, the skill in these hands and the sharpness of this mind are gifts from you. Whatever I have today, I have received.”
teach: The church in Corinth was rich in gifts and also very good at boasting. Paul asks three questions in a row: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” The psalmist says, “Not to us, LORD, not to us” — twice, as if afraid he might forget. At Lystra, when the crowd wanted to offer sacrifices to Barnabas and Paul, the two tore their clothes, rushed in among the people and cried, “We also are men of the same nature as you.”

Anyone who uses Excel knows “Trace Precedents”: click a cell and arrows appear, showing which cells fed into that number. Next time someone praises your work, press “Trace Precedents” in your heart. Who gave me this ability? Who arranged this opportunity? Which colleagues filled the gaps for me? Follow the arrows back, and they all end at the grace of God.

Giving glory to God is not saying, with false modesty, “Oh no, I’m useless” — that still keeps the focus on me. A healthy response is to say thank you sincerely, mention your partners specifically, and offer the glory to God in your heart. This kind of humility draws out humility: your team discovers there is no need to fight for credit around you, because you remember everyone. Change your mindset and you change your life — from “I did it” to “grace did it through me”.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. Shift the viewpoint from the human to the divine: everything I have, I have received. Humility draws out humility, and the whole team wins.
lessons.scene: Hana is a freelance graphic designer in Auckland. A client emails to say her brand campaign has been a huge hit, and an industry newsletter wants to interview her under the headline “The Designer Who Single-Handedly Built a Viral Campaign”. In fact the printer rescued a colour problem, and her intern came up with the key slogan. Hana is writing her reply.
q: Who is God? — “What do you have that you didn’t receive?” What does this show you about God’s generosity?
Who am I? — When praised, do you tend to accept it all, feign modesty, or honestly trace the grace?
How shall I respond? — How could Hana word her reply with genuine humility?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did many miracles, yet he said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). Every glorious work of his pointed the arrow back to the Father. If the perfect Son did this, how much more should we trace every compliment back to the Father?
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for my abilities, my opportunities and the people beside me. When I am praised, remind me to trace the source of grace — not to take it all, nor to fake modesty. Let me say thank you sincerely, remember others specifically, and offer all the glory to you in my heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List three “precedents” behind one of your recent results
When praised, say, “Thank you — and it’s also thanks to …”
Thank God specifically for one gift he has given you
lessons.noon: “Not to us, LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory” — Lord, right now I give today’s results to you.

lessons.title: Joseph, Forgotten
lessons.theme: When overlooked, humble yourself under God’s mighty hand and let no bitterness take root

v: Yet the chief cup bearer didn’t remember Joseph, but forgot him.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,
casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

lessons.still: Lift your shoulders up hard, then slowly let them drop. Tell the Lord: “Lord, I cast the hurt of being overlooked on you, because you care for me.” Repeat it once, and let your shoulders truly relax.
teach: In prison, Joseph interpreted the cupbearer’s dream and asked for just one thing: “But remember me when it is well with you.” The text answers in a single line: “Yet the chief cup bearer didn’t remember Joseph, but forgot him.” Then come the words “at the end of two full years”. Two years without a reply, without news. We cannot know what Joseph thought each night, but later he named his firstborn Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my toil.” He was not swallowed by bitterness; in God’s hands, he was being prepared.

Being overlooked at work is often subtle: the project celebration email lists everyone but you; the manager thanks every team in the meeting except the one whose report you stayed up to finish. It feels like sending a letter that lands in a spam folder. But remember: heaven’s inbox has no spam folder. “God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work” (Hebrews 6:10). Every effort you make is received, read and recorded by him.

Peter writes, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” Humbling yourself is not self-rejection; it is accepting that the timetable is in God’s hands. Bitterness is a root that starts small and grows until it troubles many (Hebrews 12:15). Casting your worries on God keeps that root from taking hold. If being overlooked has become a long-term injustice, you can raise it gently, and where needed seek help from someone you trust. But first, give your heart to the Lord who cares for you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on others or circumstances. Use the heart and rely on the Spirit, not the head and rely on yourself — the heart brings gladness, the head brings worry. Humbling yourself under God’s mighty hand means laying down your right to run your own life.
lessons.scene: Siying is a marketing executive at a consumer-goods company in Penang. The new product launch was a great success, and her manager sends a company-wide thank-you email listing more than a dozen names — but not hers, though she wrote the script for the video that went viral. A colleague forwards it: “Why aren’t you on here?” She opens a reply window and types a long paragraph. The cursor is still blinking.
q: Who is God? — The cupbearer forgot Joseph, but God did not. How does that help you know the God who “cares for you”?
Who am I? — Which recent experience of being overlooked still aches a little in your heart?
How shall I respond? — Would you advise Siying to delete that long paragraph, rewrite it, or say it another way?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus most needed friends, his disciples all left him and fled. “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). The Lord who was overlooked by everyone understands your hurt, and leads you out of bitterness.
lessons.pray: Lord who cares for me, you know the sourness and pain I feel when I am overlooked. I don’t want to pretend it doesn’t matter, and I don’t want bitterness to take root in me. Right now I cast this hurt on you. Keep me under your mighty hand, and lift me up in your time. If I need to speak up, give me gentleness and wisdom. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down today’s slight, and hand it specifically to God
Before replying to any message, wait ten minutes and pray one line
Affirm a colleague who is often overlooked too
lessons.noon: “Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” — Lord, right now I cast this hurt on you.

lessons.title: The Temperature of the Group Chat
lessons.theme: Humility draws out humility; pride provokes pride

v: When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got off her donkey, and fell before David on her face and bowed herself to the ground.
She fell at his feet and said, “On me, my lord, on me be the blame! Please let your servant speak in your ears. Hear the words of your servant.
David said to Abigail, “Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me!
Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.

lessons.still: Before you open any messages, pray: “Lord, let every word I say today bring the temperature down, not up.” Relax your jaw, then begin.
teach: Nabal insulted David: “Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse?” Pride provoked pride, and David immediately said, “Every man put on his sword!” Four hundred men set out, bent on bloodshed. Then Nabal’s wife Abigail appeared. She hurried off her donkey, fell at David’s feet and said, “On me, my lord, on me be the blame!” Her humility was like a bucket of cold water on a fire. David turned to bless God and thanked her for keeping him “from avenging myself with my own hand”.

Nothing shows this law better than a work group chat. Drop in one sarcastic remark and someone soon fires back; then come the screenshots, the “seen” with no reply, and the temperature soars. But when someone writes, “That part was my fault for not being clear — sorry,” the temperature often drops. “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Every message adjusts the thermostat of the group.

The 321 vision says that humility draws out humility and everyone wins, while pride provokes pride and both sides lose. Nabal’s pride nearly destroyed his whole household; Abigail’s humility saved everyone, and saved David from sin. Humility is the key to revival — not weak retreat, but the courage and wisdom to lay down face first. Those who humble themselves under God’s mighty hand are best able to bring peace among people.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility draws out humility and both win; pride provokes pride and both lose. Humility is the key to revival. People matter more than tasks — don’t wound a person to win an argument.
lessons.scene: Liam is a planning officer with Wellington city council. A contractor sends a furious email, copying in Liam’s manager, accusing him of delaying approval. Part of the delay really was Liam missing a document, but the contractor had also left items out. Liam has written a point-by-point rebuttal, and his cursor is resting on “Send”.
q: Who is God? — God used Abigail to keep David from revenge. What does that show you about how God guards people from sin?
Who am I? — In conflict, are you more like Nabal, David or Abigail?
How shall I respond? — How could Liam rewrite his reply to lower the temperature while still stating the facts clearly?
lessons.jesus: Humanity set its pride against God, and sin and revenge kept escalating. But Jesus humbled himself: when he was cursed, he didn’t curse back (1 Peter 2:23), and on the cross he prayed for those who crucified him. By his humility he broke the chain of retaliation and brought peace between God and people, and between people and one another.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, by your humility you broke the chain of revenge. I am often like David — insulted, and ready to reach for my sword. Teach me to be like Abigail, with the courage to own my part first and to answer gently. Today, in every group chat and every email, make me someone who lowers the temperature. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before replying in a conflict, delete one barbed sentence
Own up to one mistake of your own
Say one kind word to a colleague you’re at odds with
lessons.noon: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God” — Lord, right now let my next words lower the temperature.

mem.t: each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

lessons.title: The Lift That Went All the Way Down
lessons.theme: The mind of Christ is a mind willing to go all the way down

v: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.

lessons.still: As you step into the lift or onto the stairs, notice the moment you go up or down. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you went all the way down for me. Today let me have your mind.”
teach: Paul writes, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,” and then traces a path downwards. He was in the form of God, yet “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”. And “he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” From God to man, from man to servant, from life to death, from death to the most shameful death of all — each step lower than the last. “Emptied himself” does not mean he lost his divinity, but that he did not cling to his divine rights.

Picture a lift where everyone presses the top floor: promotion, a pay rise, a bigger office. Only one man steps in and presses the fifth basement level — and rides it all the way down. That is Jesus. He was not demoted against his will; he chose to go down, because the place he was heading for was the very bottom, where we were trapped. Workplace culture teaches us to keep pressing “up”. The mind of Christ teaches us that, for love, we can press “down”.

Adam wanted to be “like God” and reached out to grasp it. Christ was equal with God and did not grasp. That is the line between self-centredness and the self-emptied life. Pride is leaving your proper place to seize power; humility is laying down power and returning to your place. A change of mindset starts here: my position, seniority and title at work are not things I must clutch. With Christ’s mind as my mind, I am free to go down and serve the people who truly need it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving your place to seize power; humility is laying power down and returning to your place. Jesus is my example — he did not grasp; he emptied himself. In Christ, I can open my clenched hands too.
lessons.scene: Meiling has been a sales manager at a traditional manufacturing firm in Taichung for eight years. In a restructure she has been placed, for now, under a younger manager, and asked to take new recruits round the smallest, most basic customers. She feels this is simply not work for someone of her grade, and is about to email HR: “This arrangement doesn’t seem reasonable.”
q: Who is God? — Jesus “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped”. What does this show you about how he viewed his rights?
Who am I? — At work, what do you cling to most tightly: title, seniority or other people’s respect?
How shall I respond? — Should Meiling send that email? If she does, how could she write it with the mind of Christ?
lessons.jesus: The downward road did not end at the cross. Paul goes on: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Jesus went all the way down, and the Father raised him to the highest place. Those who follow him downwards will be lifted up by him in God’s time.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you were in the form of God, yet you willingly went all the way down and died on a cross for me. I confess I usually want to press “up”. Put your mind in me, so I don’t cling to titles and face. If I am given work that seems “beneath me” today, give me a willing heart, and wisdom to say honestly what I think. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the thing you cling to most at work, and give it to the Lord
Willingly do one task “below” your grade
Memorise Philippians 2:4 and say it once in the lift
lessons.noon: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” — Lord, right now let me go down willingly to serve.

lessons.title: Checking the Mirrors
lessons.theme: Do your own work well, and see the needs of others too

v: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Let each one of us please his neighbour for that which is good, to be building him up.
For even Christ didn’t please himself. But, as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”

lessons.still: Sit up and turn to look at the colleagues on either side of you, or picture their faces. Tell the Lord: “Lord, don’t let me watch only my own lane today. Let me see them too.”
teach: Paul says, do “nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself”. Then comes this week’s memory verse: “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” Notice the word “also”. Paul is not telling us to neglect our own work, but not to look only at it. He reminds the Romans, “Let each one of us please his neighbour for that which is good,” because “even Christ didn’t please himself.”

Every driver knows you cannot stare only at your own lane ahead; you must keep checking the mirrors. Look only forward and sooner or later you will clip the car beside you, or miss the ambulance coming up behind. Work is the same. There is nothing wrong with pushing hard on your own project, but if you never check your mirrors, you will miss the colleague who is about to go under, or the other department that needs a little of your experience.

“Counting others better than himself” is not low self-esteem; it is a way of seeing — noticing the worth God has placed in each person. That way of seeing changes relationships: people matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. The self-centred driver watches only his own lane; the self-emptied one checks the mirrors. It will not make your work worse; it makes the whole road safer. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — a team’s effectiveness often begins with caring for one another.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. The order of relationships is God, self, others, tasks. Not looking only to our own things means putting people before tasks.
lessons.scene: Cheng’en is a data analyst at a logistics company in Singapore. His quarterly project is due on Friday, and his year-end bonus rides on it. On Wednesday afternoon a colleague from another department comes to him for help: she presents to management tomorrow and her dashboard figures are all wrong. Fixing it will take him about three hours. Cheng’en looks at the clock, then at her.
q: Who is God? — “Even Christ didn’t please himself.” What does this show you about what mattered most to Jesus?
Who am I? — This week, how much of your time has been spent “checking the mirrors” for other people’s needs?
How shall I respond? — How could Cheng’en care for both his project and his colleague’s urgent need? What would you choose?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never looked only to his own things. When he was arrested, he healed the servant whose ear had been cut off; on the cross, he cared for his mother and gave a promise to the repentant criminal beside him. He did not please himself, and so our needs became what mattered most to him.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you did not please yourself; you always saw the needs of others. I often watch only my own lane and care only about my own performance. Give me eyes that check the mirrors, and let me see one colleague who needs help today. Give me wisdom to plan my time too, so I don’t neglect my own responsibilities. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Ask a colleague, “Is anything holding you up at the moment?”
Set aside fifteen minutes to help solve someone’s small problem
Name, in your heart, one way a colleague is better than you
lessons.noon: “Each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” — Lord, right now let me see the people around me.

lessons.title: Comments for Whoever Comes Next
lessons.theme: The sower may not reap, but in God’s eyes sower and reaper rejoice together

v: Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest?’ Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.
He who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit to eternal life, that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.
For in this the saying is true, ‘One sows, and another reaps.’
I sent you to reap that for which you haven’t laboured. Others have laboured, and you have entered into their labour.”

lessons.still: Think about the work in your hands today, and whose hands it will pass into one day. Tell the Lord: “Lord, let what I do today become someone else’s blessing tomorrow.”
teach: The disciples came back with food and found Jesus talking with a Samaritan woman; they could not understand why he wasn’t hungry. Jesus said, “Lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.” He spoke of a harvest in which “both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together”, quoting the saying, “One sows, and another reaps.” What the disciples were about to reap was other people’s labour — the prophets, John the Baptist, and the woman who had just run back into town to tell everyone. In God’s kingdom, no one starts from zero.

Good programmers write clear comments in their code: what this section does, why it was written this way, where to be careful. They know they may never meet the person who maintains that code years later, but that person will be spared many late nights because of those comments. Paving the way for others is like writing comments: it will never appear in your performance review, but it makes the road smoother for whoever comes next.

Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Denying self means being willing to sow without necessarily seeing the harvest, and without grabbing the credit for the reaping. In 235, spiritual parents are exactly this kind of people: they hand on what they have learned, so the next generation can go further than they did. Shift the viewpoint from the temporary to the eternal: in God’s eyes, sower and reaper rejoice together.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 235 reminds us to build spiritual parent-and-child relationships, where the sower gladly paves the way for the reaper. Shift the viewpoint from the temporary to the eternal: God remembers every sower.
lessons.scene: Jingyi teaches at a primary school in Kaohsiung and has been transferred mid-term. On Monday a relief teacher takes over her class. She could simply hand over the grade book and timetable — or spend the weekend writing a note on each of her thirty pupils. On Saturday evening, with a family dinner already planned, she looks at the pile of blank cards on the table.
q: Who is God? — God makes sower and reaper rejoice together. What does this show you about how he views unseen effort?
Who am I? — At work, are you more often the sower or the one reaping others’ labour? How have you responded?
How shall I respond? — How could Jingyi make a balanced decision between her family and her pupils?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). He himself is that grain. He sowed at the cross, and the three thousand at Pentecost were the harvest. The salvation we enjoy today is entirely the fruit of his labour.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the grain of wheat that fell into the earth; everything I have today is the fruit of your labour. Make me willing to sow too, paving the way for the colleagues who take over and for the next generation, without caring whether my name is on it. And keep me from neglecting my family in my busyness. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write a clear handover note for one piece of your work
Thank a senior colleague who once paved the way for you
Teach a newcomer a skill that took you a long time to learn
lessons.noon: “Both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.” — Lord, right now make me glad to sow for others.

lessons.title: A Cross Once a Day
lessons.theme: Taking up the cross daily mostly means denying self in small, unnoticed things

v: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.
For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it.
For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses or forfeits his own self?

lessons.still: Trace a small cross on your chest with your finger. Tell the Lord: “Lord, the cross I carry today may be small and ordinary. Give me strength to take it up willingly and follow you.”
teach: Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” Many manuscripts of Luke add the word “daily”, and the Chinese Bible keeps it. In that world a cross was no ornament but an instrument of execution; whoever carried one was walking to his death. To deny yourself is to say no to “I want to run my own life.” Jesus goes on: whoever wants to save his life will lose it, and “what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses or forfeits his own self?”

A pharmacy label often says: “Take once a day, after food.” The medicine works not by swallowing the whole bottle at once, but by taking it every day, on time, without a break. Carrying the cross is like that. It is not one dramatic sacrifice and then done; it is a little self-denial each day: not insisting on the last word, taking the job nobody wants, giving away a bit of credit, offering a difficult client a little more patience.

The small crosses of work rarely look like crosses; they look like inconvenience or a little unfairness. Yet it is in these small things that self-centredness is dealt with bit by bit, and the life of Christ grows bit by bit. One distinction matters: taking up the cross is willing self-denial for the Lord, not silently enduring bullying or illegal demands — in that case, seek help from someone you trust or a professional. The 920 practice bears fruit in a cross taken up once a day.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Denying self means living for Jesus, for others, not for myself. The “0” in 920 — the self-emptied life — is trained by small daily crosses, and it bears the Spirit’s “9” fruits.
lessons.scene: Jinrong runs a family restaurant in Ipoh. After closing on Sundays, someone has to clean the grease trap — filthy, stinking work, which by custom goes to the newest staff member. Tonight that young worker is slumped in a corner, exhausted, while everyone else has changed and is ready to leave. Jinrong stands in the kitchen doorway, gloves in his hand.
q: Who is God? — Jesus calls us to deny ourselves and take up our cross. What kind of following does he want?
Who am I? — In your work today, what “small cross” is most likely to appear?
How shall I respond? — Whom should Jinrong hand the gloves to? If it were you, what would you do?
lessons.jesus: Jesus carried a real cross towards Golgotha, and on the way Simon of Cyrene was seized and made to carry it after him (Luke 23:26). The cross Jesus carried bore our sin; we could never carry it. The cross he asks us to carry is the small one of following him and denying ourselves each day.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you carried the cross I could never carry. Today give me grace to take up my small cross: a little more patience, a little less score-keeping, a willingness to do what no one wants to do. And give me wisdom to tell the difference between denying myself for you and needing to say a brave no. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Take on one job today that everyone else is avoiding
In a disagreement, let go of the line you must “win” with
Tonight, recall the moment you carried a small cross
lessons.noon: “Let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” — Lord, right now I am willing to deny myself in this small thing.

lessons.title: Set the Destination
lessons.theme: For Jesus, for others, not for myself — three directions of self-denial

v: For the love of Christ compels us; because we judge thus: that one died for all, therefore all died.
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.
For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself.
For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.

lessons.still: Before work, set today’s destination in your heart, as you would on a sat-nav. Tell the Lord: “Lord, today I work for you, for others, and not for myself.”
teach: Paul says, “For the love of Christ compels us.” The word carries the sense of gripping, pressing, holding fast. What had gripped Paul? The love of the cross: “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” He tells the Romans too, “For none of us lives to himself,” and “if we live, we live to the Lord.” Self-denial is not gritting your teeth by willpower; it is what happens when Christ’s love takes hold of you.

The most important thing about a sat-nav is not how clever the route is, but whether the destination is right. With the wrong destination, going faster only gets you lost faster. Many people work tremendously hard without ever setting who they work for. The 321 vision gives three destinations: for Jesus — letting him be King and receive the glory; for others — serving our “2”; not for myself — not letting self-centredness steer. Reset them every morning, and you will not drift off course.

Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). The self-emptied life is not emptiness but entering and living out the boundless. When I no longer live for myself, I no longer have to be anxious about my own success, comparisons or reputation. Over these weeks we have learned a servant’s heart, humility and self-denial; may these three destinations become the default setting for your working life.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Denying self means living for Jesus, for others, not for myself. The self-emptied life is “no longer I, but Christ lives in me”; it is not losing yourself but entering and living out the boundless.
lessons.scene: Aroha is a night-shift carer at a rest home in Rotorua. At two in the morning she has just sat down with a cup of tea when an elderly resident who cannot sleep presses the call bell for the fifth time. There is nothing urgent; she just wants someone to talk to. Aroha’s feet ache, her tea is still steaming, and the call light comes on again.
q: Who is God? — “The love of Christ compels us.” How can this love become the driving force of your work?
Who am I? — If you check honestly, where is today’s “destination” for your work set?
How shall I respond? — How can Aroha live out the three destinations while also looking after herself?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never lived for himself. He prayed, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He lived for the Father and died for us. “Who loved me and gave himself up for me” — it is this Lord, who gave himself for me, whose love moves me to live for him and for others.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you gave yourself up for me, and your love has taken hold of me. Today I reset my destination: for you, for others, not for myself. When I am tired and want to think only of myself, let your love compel me again. And teach me to rest as I serve, because I belong to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Say in the morning: “For Jesus, for others, not for myself”
For one task, think specifically about whom it serves
When tired, pray one line, then respond to one need
lessons.noon: “If we live, we live to the Lord.” — Lord, right now I reset my destination and live for you.

mem.t: His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

lessons.title: Five, Two and One
lessons.theme: How much talent you have is not the point; knowing your master and being faithful is

v: “For it is like a man going into another country, who called his own servants and entrusted his goods to them.
To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his own ability. Then he went on his journey.
Immediately he who received the five talents went and traded with them, and made another five talents.
In the same way, he also who got the two gained another two.
But he who received the one talent went away and dug in the earth and hid his lord’s money.
“He also who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man, reaping where you didn’t sow, and gathering where you didn’t scatter.
I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.’
“But his lord answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant. You knew that I reap where I didn’t sow, and gather where I didn’t scatter.

lessons.still: Open today’s calendar and glance over it. Tell the Lord: “Lord, this day, this work and these abilities are all entrusted to me by you. I won’t compare; I only ask to be faithful.”
teach: A man about to travel abroad gives his servants money, “to each according to his own ability”: five talents, two, and one. The master knows each servant’s capacity, and entrusts each differently. The one with five “immediately” went and traded, and the one with two did the same; but the one with one talent dug a hole and hid it. When the master returns, the servant’s explanation exposes the root of the problem: “I knew you that you are a hard man … I was afraid.” He had misjudged his master, so fear bound him and he did nothing at all.

Every year a company sets budgets, and departments receive very different amounts. Yet at the year-end review a good manager doesn’t only ask who spent or earned the most, but whether each department used its budget well. The one-talent servant did not lose because his budget was small, but because he locked it in a drawer and never touched it, afraid of being blamed. Many people “bury their talent” at work — not out of laziness, but from fear of mistakes, of comparison, of not being good enough.

The key to this parable is not how much I receive, but how I know my master. If I think God is a harsh boss, I will only protect myself; if I know he is good, I can invest boldly. The servants with five and two received exactly the same praise: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” God does not compare; he looks for faithfulness. Change your mindset and you change your life — from fear of failing to bold offering, grounded in trust.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset and you change your life. Misjudge your master and you live in fear; know God’s goodness and you can give yourself faithfully at work. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on comparison with others.
lessons.scene: Weilun has just finished his first year at an advertising agency. The others who joined with him were given big brands; he got a small account for a neighbourhood bakery. In this afternoon’s brainstorm he could simply reuse last year’s template, or he could take the trouble to learn this bakery’s story. He opens the folder, and the template is the first file.
q: Who is God? — The master entrusted “to each according to his own ability”. What does that show you about how God knows you?
Who am I? — Is there a “buried talent” in your life that you have never used because you were afraid?
How shall I respond? — Should Weilun open the template or start afresh? And what is the “one talent” in your hands?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the truly good and faithful servant. The Father entrusted him with the great work of redemption, and he hid nothing, remaining faithful all the way to the cross. Because of his faithfulness, we — servants who are often afraid and often bury what we’ve been given — are invited to “enter into the joy of your lord”.
lessons.pray: Good Lord, thank you for entrusting work to me according to my ability. I confess I often compare myself with others, and often bury my gifts out of fear. Let me know your goodness more deeply, so I no longer live in fear. Whatever the size of the work in my hands today, let me faithfully put it to work. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List three things entrusted to you, and give thanks for them
Take the first step today on something you’ve been afraid to start
Don’t compare; just ask, “Have I been faithful?”
lessons.noon: “You have been faithful over a few things” — Lord, right now I won’t compare; I only ask to be faithful in what is in my hands.

lessons.title: The Faithfulness of One Bolt
lessons.theme: Great things are built from a thousand very small ones

v: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?

lessons.still: Look at the smallest thing on your desk — a pen, a paper clip. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you value even the smallest things. Today let me be faithful in small things.”
teach: After the parable of the dishonest manager, Jesus states a principle: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” Then he speaks of money, and of “that which is another’s”: if you have not been faithful with what belongs to someone else, who will give you what is your own? Character does not suddenly appear on the big occasion; it is formed little by little in small places.

Aircraft maintenance engineers know that a passenger jet holds thousands upon thousands of bolts, and each must be tightened to the specified torque, signed off and double-checked. No one makes the news for tightening one bolt properly, but one loose bolt could bring down the whole plane. Faithfulness at work is the same: a receipt on an expense claim, those ten minutes of working time, a ream of the company’s paper — each one is that bolt.

“That which is another’s” includes the company’s time, its resources and its clients’ trust. Faithfulness in small things is not legalistic nit-picking; it comes from knowing that I am a steward, not the owner. It is a change of mindset: from “no one will notice” to “the Master sees everything”. One of the fruits of the Spirit is faithfulness, and it grows precisely in the smallest things. Faithfulness like this lets people see in you the God who is faithful.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Bible is my standard. Faithfulness is among the fruit of the Spirit; change from the inside out often begins with the smallest details of daily life, and in the end shapes relationships and ministry.
lessons.scene: Peishan is a sales representative for a medical-device company in Kuala Lumpur. At month’s end, everyone in her team rounds their taxi fares up a little when claiming expenses. Her supervisor laughs: “Everyone does it. Finance never checks — call it an allowance.” Her receipt says twenty-eight ringgit, and the box on the claim form is still empty.
q: Who is God? — Jesus says the one faithful in very little is faithful in much. What does this show you about what God values?
Who am I? — In your work, which “bolt” are you most tempted to leave loose?
How shall I respond? — How should Peishan fill in that box? And how might she respond gently to her supervisor and colleagues?
lessons.jesus: Before his public ministry, Jesus went back to Nazareth, “was subject to them”, grew up in an ordinary home, and “increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men” (Luke 2:51–52). He was faithful in the smallest things, and so we see that the faithful Son pleased the Father in ordinary days too.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, you see me in the smallest things. I confess that sometimes I think small things don’t matter because everyone else does them. Help me remember that I am a steward, not the owner. Today, in my expense claims, my time and every small task, let me be faithful, as if tightening every bolt. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Fill in every claim, timesheet and form accurately today
Finish one “good enough” task properly instead
Spend ten fewer minutes on your phone during work hours
lessons.noon: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” — Lord, right now let me be faithful in this small thing.

lessons.title: The Woman Who Gleaned
lessons.theme: Diligence is not for being seen, yet God so often sees it

v: Ruth the Moabitess said to Naomi, “Let me now go to the field, and glean amongst the ears of grain after him in whose sight I find favour.” She said to her, “Go, my daughter.”
She went, and came and gleaned in the field after the reapers; and she happened to come to the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, who was of the family of Elimelech.

Boaz answered her, “I have been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, and how you have left your father, your mother, and the land of your birth, and have come to a people that you didn’t know before.
May the LORD repay your work, and a full reward be given to you from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”

lessons.still: Roll up your sleeves or tie back your hair, as if starting a day’s work. Tell the Lord: “Lord, however basic my work is today, I am working in your field.”
teach: Ruth was a widow and a foreigner from Moab who had followed her mother-in-law back to Bethlehem with nothing. She offered, “Let me now go to the field,” to glean behind the reapers — the grain the law left for the poor and the foreigner (Leviticus 19:9–10), the most basic work there was. The overseer described her: “She came, and has continued even from the morning until now, except that she rested a little in the house.” The text says she “happened to come” to Boaz’s field. It looked like chance; it was God’s arrangement.

Think of the student who restocks a supermarket on the night shift: filling every shelf, clearing out-of-date stock, so that when customers walk in at dawn, the shelves are neat — and no one wonders who did it. Ruth’s work was like that: no applause, no promotion, just one bundle of grain after another. Yet her diligence was seen. Boaz said, “I have been told all about what you have done.”

Diligence is not for being seen; it is because we are in God’s field. Boaz blessed her: “May the LORD repay your work.” Ruth later became the great-grandmother of David and entered the family line of the Messiah. Success is not proof, and failure is not condemnation; God sees and uses faithfulness in the most basic roles. This is life first, then relationships, then ministry — God first built her life, then brought relationships and blessing.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Shift the viewpoint from the temporary to the eternal: in God’s hands, a bundle of gleaned grain became part of the story of salvation.
lessons.scene: Haiyan is in her forties. After her factory closed, she became a picker at an e-commerce warehouse in Hangzhou. Just before the end of her shift she finds that the previous shift labelled a whole batch wrongly; relabelling will take twenty unpaid minutes. A young colleague beside her says, “You didn’t do it. Why bother being so careful? No one’s watching.” She glances at her watch.
q: Who is God? — Ruth “happened to come” to Boaz’s field, yet it was God’s arrangement. How does that help you know his guidance?
Who am I? — In basic, unnoticed work, is your diligence the same as when you are being watched?
How shall I respond? — Should Haiyan stay to relabel? How might she answer her young colleague?
lessons.jesus: Boaz was Ruth’s close relative and redeemer: he redeemed the family land, married her, and gave a destitute foreign widow a home. Jesus is our greater Redeemer. He gave himself to bring us — gleaners at the edge of the field — into his household, to be his bride.
lessons.pray: Lord who sees me, thank you that you value even the most basic work. What I do today may go unnoticed, but I know I am gleaning in your field. Make me diligent and humble like Ruth, not for applause but for you. And in what looks like chance, lead me to meet your arrangement. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Do today’s most basic task as work in the Lord’s field
When you find someone else’s mistake, help fix it first
Say thank you to a colleague in a frontline role
lessons.noon: “May the LORD repay your work” — Lord, right now I work diligently in your field.

lessons.title: The Green ‘Online’ Light
lessons.theme: The truth about the quality of your work shows when no one is watching

v: Servants, obey in all things those who are your masters according to the flesh, not just when they are looking, as men pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing God.
And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,
knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.

lessons.still: If you work from home, glance at your webcam; if you’re in the office, look at a corner no one pays attention to. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you are always watching. Today I work for you.”
teach: Paul writes to believers who were servants: obey “not just when they are looking, as men pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing God.” Working only when watched means being diligent while the master is there and slacking once he leaves. Paul is not endorsing slavery; in the most unjust of situations, he gives a new motive for work: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,” because “you serve the Lord Christ.”

Anyone who works remotely knows the green dot on the messaging app: as long as it is lit, you look “online”. Some people learn to keep the dot green while doing something else entirely. The green light may fool a manager, but not God. Working only when watched is a green-dot way of working; working heartily means that even when the dot is grey and no one is looking, the quality of your work is just the same.

Shift the viewpoint from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly. When we know that “from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance”, work is no longer only for appraisals, bonuses or the boss’s eye. This is not a call to overwork or to forget rest; it is a call to genuine quality. Diligence where no one sees is God’s quietest form of worship, and it builds God’s order in the workplace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift the viewpoint from the human to the divine, from the temporary to the eternal. Work quality is most real when no one is watching; working for the Lord builds God’s order at work.
lessons.scene: Tevita does waterproofing on a housing site in Auckland. The foreman is pushing him hard to finish the bathroom membranes today. The specification calls for two coats, with drying time between, but once the tiles go down no one will ever see how many coats are underneath. Skipping one would save half a day. Tevita holds his roller, looking at a first coat that is only half dry.
q: Who is God? — “You serve the Lord Christ.” What kind of Lord is the one who is always watching?
Who am I? — If no one checked and there were no appraisal, how would the quality of your work change?
How shall I respond? — How can Tevita respond to the foreman’s pressure and still keep the quality no one will see?
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught us to do good in secret, and “your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:4). He often prayed alone, early in the morning or on the mountain; he lived before the Father, not before the crowds. This Lord, faithful in secret, invites us to work for the Father in secret too.
lessons.pray: Father who sees in secret, you see the work no one else sees. I confess that sometimes I only try hard when I am being watched. Help me to work heartily, as for you. Today, whether or not anyone checks and whether or not anyone knows, let the quality of my work be real, because the one I serve is the Lord Christ. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pick one task no one will check, and do it to standard
Drop the urge to perform; focus fully for fifteen minutes
Before leaving, ask: which task did I do for the Lord today?
lessons.noon: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord” — Lord, right now I do this task well for you.

lessons.title: The Factory in the Living Room
lessons.theme: Give the little in your hands to the Lord; he gives thanks, breaks it and shares it with many

v: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,
“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these amongst so many?”
Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand.
Jesus took the loaves, and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down, likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.

lessons.still: Open your hands and think of the most ordinary ability or resource you have. Tell the Lord: “Lord, these are my five loaves and two fish. It isn’t much, but I give it to you.”
teach: Five thousand people are out in the countryside. Philip has done the sums: even two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough. Andrew finds a boy with five barley loaves and two fish, but says, “What are these amongst so many?” Barley loaves were usually the bread of ordinary, poorer people, and there were only five. Yet Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” He took the loaves, gave thanks and distributed them, and the fish likewise. Everyone ate their fill, and twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered.

In Taiwan’s early boom years there was a saying: “The living room is the factory.” Countless families turned their living rooms into small workshops, taking on one small order after another — Christmas lights, umbrellas, toy parts. Each was tiny, but tens of thousands of living rooms together powered an economy for a generation. God’s kingdom works like that.
