He doesn’t wait for you to own a large factory; he wants the small order in your living room, placed in his hands.

These weeks we have learned a servant’s heart: serving, humility, self-denial and faithfulness. You may feel your abilities are ordinary, your position small, your influence limited, and ask with Andrew, “What are these?” But God does not despise the day of small things (Zechariah 4:10). Give the little in your hands to the Lord — a skill, some time, a sincere heart — and he will give thanks, break it, and let it feed people you never imagined. The point is not how much bread there is, but whose hands it is in.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on yourself, others or circumstances. Change the mindset from “I only have this little” to “this little is in the Lord’s hands”. Let Jesus be King, and let him receive all the glory.
lessons.scene: Ruilin spent fifteen years as a purchasing manager at a multinational in Shanghai, and was made redundant six months ago. Today, on a job site, he sees that a small social-welfare charity needs an administrative officer. The salary is a third of what he used to earn, but they need someone who understands purchasing and cost control. His CV is uploaded, and his cursor rests on “Submit application”.
q: Who is God? — Jesus took a boy’s five loaves and two fish and gave thanks. What does this show you about how he sees small offerings?
Who am I? — Do you often feel your “five loaves and two fish” are too little to mention?
How shall I respond? — Should Ruilin press “Submit”? What small thing can you place in the Lord’s hands today?
lessons.jesus: After feeding the five thousand, Jesus said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). He did not only break the bread; later he let his own body be broken to become our bread. He himself is the gift that was given, broken, and shared to feed multitudes.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the bread of life, and your body was broken for me. What I have is little, and I often think, “What is this?” Today I place my skills, my time and my experience in your hands. Please give thanks, break them, and make them a blessing to others. I won’t look at how much bread there is, only at whose hands it is in. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down your “five loaves and two fish”: one skill or resource
Use it to do one small thing for a colleague or client
Pray, placing today’s work into the Lord’s hands
lessons.noon: “Jesus took the loaves, and having given thanks, he distributed” — Lord, right now I give you the little in my hands.

mem.t: Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesnt brag, is not proud.

lessons.title: Love's Spec Sheet
lessons.theme: Love is not a passing feeling but a specification we carry out at work every day

v: Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,
doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;
doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;
bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.

lessons.still: Before you leave home, rest your open hands on your knees and say slowly, “Love is patient and is kind.” Then tell the Lord, “Lord, my patience will run out today. Please lend me your love.” Take three deep breaths, and stand up.
teach: The church in Corinth was rich in gifts: tongues, prophecy, knowledge. Yet it was split into factions and full of comparison. Right in the middle of two chapters about spiritual gifts, Paul sets this ‘poem of love’. Notice that almost every line is a verb or a negative: love doesn’t envy, doesn’t brag, doesn’t seek its own way, takes no account of evil. Love here is not a flutter of the heart but a chain of choices. It begins with ‘patient’ and ends with ‘endures all things’, like two door frames holding every kindness inside patience.

Every engineer knows the spec sheet. Whether a product passes is not decided by the advert, but by whether it still meets specification under heat, vibration and long hours of running. First Corinthians 13 is love’s spec sheet. Interrupted in a meeting: ‘is not provoked’. A colleague promoted: ‘doesn’t envy’. Your presentation praised: ‘doesn’t brag’. A junior making the same mistake for the third time: ‘takes no account of evil’. The workplace is love’s testing lab, running tests every day and printing a report every evening.

Read the spec and we quickly find we fail it. That is the point. This love is not squeezed out of us; it is fruit the Spirit bears. The self-centred life always ‘seeks its own way’, so it envies, flares up and keeps score. When we let Jesus be King and return to our proper place, his love can flow through us. Change your thinking and your life changes: from ‘I’ll treat people well once they treat me well’ to ‘The Lord loved me first, so I can love first.’
lessons.light: 321 Light: In 920, the ‘0’ is the self-emptied life. ‘Doesn’t seek its own way’ is a portrait of it. When I stop trying to be lord of my own life, the Spirit bears the fruit of love in my relationship with every ‘2’. People matter more than tasks: better to spend five extra minutes than to wound someone for the sake of a task.
lessons.scene: Zonghan leads a software team at a semiconductor equipment firm in Hsinchu. For the third time this month, the new hire, Xiao Guo, has set the test parameters wrong, and a whole batch of machines must be rerun. At seven on Friday evening, Zonghan has typed into the team chat, “Are you even using your brain?” The cursor blinks beside ‘Send’.
q: Who is God? — From the words ‘love is patient’, what do you see of how God treats you when you stumble again and again?
Who am I? — Of the many marks of love in this passage, which one do you most often ‘fail the test’ on at work?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zonghan, how would you rewrite that message so it names the problem without wounding the person?
lessons.jesus: Put ‘Jesus’ in place of ‘love’ in this passage and every line holds true: Jesus is patient and kind; Jesus doesn’t seek his own way and takes no account of evil. He never gave up on Peter through all his failures, and on the cross he prayed for those who crucified him. He is not only love’s example; he is love itself, and his righteousness covers every place where we fail the test.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are patient and kind with me. I confess that at work I am often impatient, quick to keep score, and quietly envious of others’ success. Fill me with your love today. When colleagues make mistakes, meetings drag on and messages keep pinging, help me pause first, see people with your eyes, and only then speak. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Wait three minutes and reread before sending any critical message
Find a colleague who recently made a mistake and affirm one specific strength
Set ‘Love is patient’ as your phone’s wallpaper today
lessons.noon: “Love is patient and is kind” — Lord, right now I hand you the anger rising in me; lend me your patience.

lessons.title: Wounded Off the Org Chart
lessons.theme: A neighbour is not someone I choose to love but someone I choose to become

v: But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbour?”
Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell amongst robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he travelled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbour to him who fell amongst the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

lessons.still: Before you head out, look at your hands and say, “Lord, these hands are not only for finishing my own work today. They are ready to lift someone up. Open my eyes to see my neighbour today.”
teach: When the lawyer asked, ‘Who is my neighbour?’ he wanted to draw a line: who is inside my responsibility and who is outside it. Jesus turned the question over with a story. The priest and the Levite may have had reasons: a schedule, a concern about ritual purity. Both ‘saw him’, and both ‘passed by on the other side’. The Samaritan, an outsider in Jewish eyes, ‘was moved with compassion’. He bandaged the man, set him on his own animal, took him to an inn and paid two denarii in advance. Then Jesus asked: who was a neighbour to him? The question moved from ‘Who deserves my love?’ to ‘Whose neighbour am I willing to become?’

Every company has an org chart, its solid and dotted lines showing who reports to whom. The priest and the Levite walked by the org chart: not my department, not my report, not in my job description. The Samaritan saw a line the chart never drew. In hospitals, factories and offices, someone is always lying on the road between departments: the colleague just made redundant, the new hire nobody is training, the migrant worker far from home, the cleaner who comes in before dawn. They are not on your org chart, but they are on God’s map.

Loving a neighbour costs something: time, oil and wine, two denarii, and a promise to follow up: ‘I will repay you when I return.’ The self-centred life calculates, ‘What do I get for helping?’ The self-emptied life only asks, ‘What does he need?’ We do not earn eternal life by being good Samaritans. Because the true Saviour stopped for us first, we find strength to stop for others. Jesus says, ‘Go and do likewise.’ Your workplace today is the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, self, others, tasks. The priest and the Levite put the task ahead of the person; the Samaritan showed that people matter more than tasks. 920 reminds me that everyone connected to me is my ‘2’, including the one who isn’t on my org chart.
lessons.scene: Huiru is a nurse on a medical ward at a hospital in Taichung. She has just handed over and is about to leave when she sees Xiaoyun, a new nurse loaned from another unit, crying in the supply room, clutching a medication record with an error on it. Huiru has been on her feet for ten hours and her child is waiting at after-school care. Her hand is on the door handle. She hesitates.
q: Who is God? — The Samaritan ‘was moved with compassion’. What does this show you of God’s heart for the wounded?
Who am I? — Are you more like the priest, the Levite or the Samaritan? What reason do you most often give for passing by on the other side?
How shall I respond? — If you were Huiru, what could she do for Xiaoyun without neglecting her own family?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself is the truest neighbour. We had fallen into the hands of sin and death, and he did not pass by on the other side. He came down from heaven, walked right up to us, healed our wounds with his own blood, paid every cost for us, and promised to come again. Only those loved like this can love others like this.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that when I lay by the roadside, you did not pass by on the other side. Open my eyes to the new hire no one notices and the colleague who has been left out. Give me wisdom to know how much time and strength I can offer today, and courage to stop and be a neighbour with a kind word or a cup of tea. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Ask someone from another team, “How are you really?” and listen
Write down the name of someone often overlooked at work, and pray for them
Answer one question a new hire feels too shy to ask
lessons.noon: “When he saw him, he was moved with compassion” — Lord, right now let me see the person near me who needs help.

lessons.title: The Sun on His Desk Too
lessons.theme: The Father’s love doesn’t pick favourites, and his children learn to love the hard to love

v: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy.’
But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,
that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.
For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
If you only greet your friends, what more do you do than others? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.

lessons.still: Before work, picture the colleague who gives you the biggest headache. Don’t push the picture away. Breathe in deeply and say softly, “Father, your sun shines on him too. Teach me today to see him through your eyes.”
teach: ‘Love your neighbour’ comes from the spirit of the law (Leviticus 19:18); ‘hate your enemy’ was a conclusion people added themselves. Jesus says, ‘Love your enemies… and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you.’ The reason is not that enemies deserve love, but that this is what the Father is like: ‘he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.’ Even tax collectors return favours. God’s children are called to another kind of love, one that doesn’t depend on the other person’s performance.

Office ‘enemies’ rarely carry knives. They take credit for your work, leave your messages on read, or casually undercut you in front of the boss. Yet the Father’s love is like a building’s central air conditioning: it doesn’t stop cooling a desk because the person sitting there is difficult. Loving enemies doesn’t mean pretending nothing happened, abandoning boundaries or tolerating injustice. It means not letting their wrong decide my response. Praying for them is the first and most practical step: it is very hard to bless someone and keep hating them at the same time.

‘You shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.’ In context, ‘perfect’ means love that is complete, not love for only half the people around us. Pride provokes pride: you kick me, I punch back, and both of us lose. Humility draws out humility: when I lay down my right to retaliate, return to my place as a creature and let God be God and Judge, the relationship has room to turn. This isn’t gritting our teeth; it is Christ living out his love in us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-centred life insists on being its own lord and settling its own scores; the self-emptied life hands judgement to God and returns to its proper place. Humility draws out humility. Praying for a hard-to-love colleague lays the first brick in building God’s order at work.
lessons.scene: Jason works in sales for a logistics tech company in Singapore. Last week, at the quarterly meeting, his colleague Kelvin described the big client Jason had chased for six months as “something we followed up together”, and the manager praised Kelvin on the spot. Today Kelvin’s quoting system has crashed, the client needs the quote in an hour, and Jason is the only one on the team who can fix it.
q: Who is God? — The Father ‘makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good’. How does this reshape what you know of his heart?
Who am I? — Do you keep a workplace ‘blacklist’ in your heart? How do the people on it affect your moods and your work?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jason, how would you answer Kelvin’s call for help? And how would you deal with the stolen credit?
lessons.jesus: Nailed to the cross, Jesus prayed for those who nailed him there: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He did not only teach love for enemies; he loved his enemies. Scripture says that ‘while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son’ (Romans 5:10). We are enemies who were loved first, and so we can learn to love ours.
lessons.pray: Father, your sun shines on the colleague who hurts me too. I confess there is resentment in me, a sense of unfairness, even a secret hope that he fails. Heal my heart and teach me to pray blessing over him. Give me wisdom to speak the truth when needed and to set healthy boundaries, without letting bitterness take root in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Spend one minute praying blessing over your hardest colleague by name
Say nothing negative about them behind their back today
Find a chance to do them one small kindness
lessons.noon: “Pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” — Lord, right now I bring that colleague’s name before you.

lessons.title: Love Is More Than a Like
lessons.theme: Real love moves from words to deeds, from appearances to truth

v: By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

lessons.still: Before you pick up your phone, turn it face down on the table. Put your palms together and say, “Lord, you laid down your life for me; you didn’t just say you loved me. Today, let my love grow hands and feet.”
teach: John wrote this letter as an elderly apostle, calling believers ‘my little children’ like a father coaching his family. He defines love: ‘By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us.’ The standard of love is not our feelings but the cross. Then he brings that lofty truth down to the most ordinary place: when you see a brother in need, do you open up, or close your ‘heart of compassion against him’? Finally he says, ‘let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.’

In the age of social media, love easily shrinks to a ‘like’. A colleague’s parent is in hospital; we drop a ‘stay strong’ sticker in the group chat, type ‘praying for you’, and scroll on. A like costs nothing and changes nothing in our schedule. The love John describes has to log off and go out. At work, love in deed might mean covering a grieving colleague’s report for a day, bringing dinner to a teammate working late, or naming someone else’s contribution in front of the boss. Love in truth means no pretence and no performance, even when no one is watching.

‘Laying down our lives’ sounds distant, but it usually begins with laying down a little: twenty minutes of lunch break, part of a weekend plan, the attitude that says ‘not my problem’. Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for self. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: as Christ’s life grows in us, love naturally grows hands and feet, and becomes a blessing colleagues can see and touch.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your thinking and your life changes; change your life and your daily living changes. Love that stays only an idea has not yet become a way of life. Of the eight steps, ‘practice’ is the one that carries love from words into deeds.
lessons.scene: Lihua supervises a production line at an electronics factory in Penang. Ani, an Indonesian operator on her line, has been distracted for days. Lihua has heard that Ani’s mother has fallen ill back home, but Ani can’t take long leave and can’t really afford the airfare. At lunch, another supervisor in the pantry says, “Let’s just pray for her.” Lihua is holding the mid-year bonus she has just received, her mind turning it over and over.
q: Who is God? — ‘He laid down his life for us.’ What does this show you about the kind of love God has?
Who am I? — Does your love more often stop at ‘word and tongue’, or reach ‘deed and truth’?
How shall I respond? — If you were Lihua, how could you help Ani in practical ways besides praying? Who could you invite to help with you?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ love was never empty talk. He reached out and touched people with leprosy, fed five thousand, stooped to wash his disciples’ feet, and finally laid down his life on the cross. The Word became flesh: love took on flesh and blood. He didn’t send a message from heaven saying ‘I love you’. He came himself.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you laid down your life for me and showed me what love is. I confess that I often care only with my mouth while being stingy with my time, energy and money. Today open my eyes to my colleagues’ real needs, and give me wisdom and courage to carry your love into their hands with a meal, a helping hand, or a sincere word of thanks. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: After saying “praying for you”, add one concrete act of help
Take one small task off a busy colleague’s plate
Name a colleague’s specific contribution to your manager or team
lessons.noon: “Let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” — Lord, right now let my love grow hands and feet.

lessons.title: Who Is My ‘2’?
lessons.theme: Find my ‘2’ at work and do one act of love for them today

v: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

lessons.still: Before work, close your eyes and let three colleagues’ faces come to mind. Say each name quietly in your heart, and pray, “Lord, these are the people you have placed beside me. Today, make me a blessing to them.”
teach: At the Last Supper, before leaving this world, Jesus gave his disciples ‘a new commandment’: ‘Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.’ Loving others wasn’t new; the standard was: the way Jesus loves us. He added that the world would recognise his disciples not by titles or attendance records, but ‘if you have love for one another’. Paul lists this love as the first fruit of the Spirit. Fruit is not a factory product rushed out on deadline; it is what a life naturally bears.

321’s ‘920’ is a simple formula for living: everyone connected to me is my ‘2’; I practise the self-emptied life, the ‘0’; and in those relationships the Spirit bears the ‘9’ fruits. Your ‘2’ might be the colleague at the next desk, the courier who collects your parcels, the boss who gives you headaches, or the shop assistant downstairs. It is like the ‘favourites’ list on your phone: that list decides who you talk to most each day, and where your love most often flows.

This week we read love’s spec sheet, noticed the wounded by the road, learned to love the hard to love, and let love grow hands and feet. Today, gather it into one action: choose one ‘2’ and do one act of love for them. It needn’t be grand, only real. In the eight steps, ‘practice’ is followed by ‘review, correction, repetition’; love is practised again and again. When you love like this, you are not ticking off a task; you are letting people recognise Jesus in you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 920 is love’s formula for life: the ‘2’ is the person, the ‘0’ is the self-emptied life, the ‘9’ is the fruit of the Spirit. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: when the self-emptied life grows, every relationship at work becomes a field for fruit.
lessons.scene: Zhiqiang runs a kopitiam-style café in Kuala Lumpur with twelve staff. After closing one evening, he sits at the till, opens a notebook and, as his small-group leader suggested, starts writing ‘My 2s’. At the fifth name he stops: Ah Ken, who washes the dishes, has worked there for three years, and Zhiqiang has never once had a proper conversation with him.
q: Who is God? — Jesus said, ‘Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.’ How has he loved you?
Who am I? — On your workplace list, which ‘2’ do you most often overlook?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zhiqiang, what one concrete act of love would you do for Ah Ken tomorrow?
lessons.jesus: Just before giving this new commandment, Jesus had stooped to wash his disciples’ feet. He knew who would betray him and who would deny him, yet ‘he loved them to the end’ (John 13:1). Our list of ‘2s’ includes people who are hard to love, but our love doesn’t come from ourselves. It comes from the Lord who loved us to the end first.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for the people you have placed in my work; each of them is my ‘2’. Help me to see not only the progress of tasks, but people’s needs. Today let your Spirit bear the fruit of love in me, so that I do one real act of love for a colleague and they catch a glimpse of you in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down five ‘2s’ from your workplace
Choose one and do an act of love for them today
Before leaving work, pray one sentence for each of the five
lessons.noon: “Just as I have loved you, you also love one another” — Lord, right now bring my ‘2’ to mind, and help me love them.

mem.t: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”

lessons.title: Route Recalculated
lessons.theme: Circumstances may chain me, but they cannot chain the gospel or steal my joy in the Lord

v: Now I desire to have you know, brothers, that the things which happened to me have turned out rather to the progress of the Good News,
so that it became evident to the whole palace guard, and to all the rest, that my bonds are in Christ,
and that most of the brothers in the Lord, being confident through my bonds, are more abundantly bold to speak the word of God without fear.
Some indeed preach Christ even out of envy and strife, and some also out of good will.
The former insincerely preach Christ from selfish ambition, thinking that they add affliction to my chains;
but the latter out of love, knowing that I am appointed for the defence of the Good News.
What does it matter? Only that in every way, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed. I rejoice in this, yes, and will rejoice.

lessons.still: Before you leave, press your wrists together as if bound, and hold them for five seconds. Then release them and say to the Lord, “Lord, whatever limits me today, you still reign. I place my situation in your hands.”
teach: When Paul wrote to the Philippians, he was in chains with an uncertain future, while others preached ‘out of envy and strife’, hoping to ‘add affliction to my chains’. Most of us would have written a letter of complaint. Paul writes instead that ‘the things which happened to me have turned out rather to the progress of the Good News.’ The palace guard heard about Christ, and timid believers grew bold. As for those with mixed motives, he says, ‘What does it matter? Only that in every way… Christ is proclaimed. I rejoice in this, yes, and will rejoice.’

Every driver knows the satnav’s calm voice: ‘Route recalculated.’ You take a wrong turn or hit a closed road, and it doesn’t scold you; it simply finds another way to your destination from where you are now. In God’s hands, Paul’s chains were a recalculation. He couldn’t go where he had planned, but God sent him into the palace guard, carrying the gospel into the heart of Rome. Being transferred, sidelined or posted to the branch nobody wants may be one of God’s recalculated routes too.

The secret of Paul’s joy is that his focus was not on himself. With the focus on self, chains, misunderstanding and someone stealing the limelight all breed bitterness. With the focus on Jesus, he can say, ‘What does it matter?’ This is the joy of the self-emptied life: not ‘I must be seen and affirmed’, but ‘Christ must be proclaimed.’ The view shifts from the temporary to the eternal, from earth to heaven. The circumstances stay the same, but the heart is set free.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep the focus on Jesus, not on self, others or circumstances. Paul’s joy did not come from better conditions but from letting Jesus receive all the glory. As long as Christ is lifted up, even chains can become channels for the gospel.
lessons.scene: Nurul is a credit officer at a bank’s headquarters in Kuala Lumpur, and her performance has always been excellent. This month she is suddenly transferred to a small-town branch on the east coast, and colleagues whisper that she has been ‘sent into exile’. On her first day, she sits in the quiet office watching the rain, with a friend’s message on her phone: “You’re not just going to accept this, are you?”
q: Who is God? — Paul’s chains became a channel for the gospel. What does this show you of how God rules over situations people call bad?
Who am I? — When your work route is ‘recalculated’, does your focus usually fall on yourself, on others, or on Jesus?
How shall I respond? — If you were Nurul, how could she look for God’s purpose in her new branch?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was bound, tried and crucified. Everything seemed out of control, yet God accomplished salvation through it. Scripture says that ‘for the joy that was set before him’ he ‘endured the cross, despising its shame’ (Hebrews 12:2). He saw the glory beyond the suffering, and so he could obey the Father even in chains.
lessons.pray: Lord, you know my situation today: some arrangements I don’t understand, and some people’s motives have hurt me. Turn my eyes away from myself and towards you. In this place of limits, let me still see your work, and let the office I am in hear about Christ because I am here. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one ‘unwelcome’ arrangement, and beside it: What does it matter?
Find one chance to bless someone in your current role
Don’t complain to anyone about your situation today
lessons.noon: “I rejoice in this, yes, and will rejoice” — Lord, right now I choose to fix my focus on you.

lessons.title: A Dashboard Full of Red
lessons.theme: When every number fails, I can still be joyful in the God of my salvation

v: For even though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines, the labour of the olive fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls,
yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!
The LORD, the Lord, is my strength. He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and enables me to go in high places. For the music director, on my stringed instruments.

lessons.still: When you sit down, don’t open any reports yet. Rest your hands on the desk and say, “Lord, even if every number looks bad today, you are still the God of my salvation. I give you my heart first, then I’ll open the day.”
teach: Habakkuk was a prophet bold enough to argue with God. He saw violence in the land, then heard that God would raise up the Babylonians to discipline his people, and his heart was full of questions. Yet in his final chapter he writes a song: the fig tree doesn’t flourish, the vines bear no fruit, the olive fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are gone, the stalls are empty. For an agricultural society, that is every source of income at zero. Even so, he says, ‘yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!’

Modern companies run dashboards: revenue, margin, conversion, cash flow. Green means healthy; red means warning. Habakkuk describes a dashboard with all six indicators flashing red. His joy is not pretending not to see the red, nor positive thinking that relabels red as green. He admits that everything has failed, yet finds, beyond the dashboard, a foundation that never flashes red: ‘The LORD, the Lord, is my strength.’

The key to this song lies in two small words: ‘even though’ and ‘yet’. Self-centred joy runs on ‘because’: because sales are up, because I was praised, I am happy. Godly joy runs on ‘even though… yet’: even though circumstances won’t cooperate, yet God is still God. Success is not proof that God loves me, and failure is not a verdict that he has rejected me. When we return to our place and let God be God, ‘he makes my feet like deer’s feet’, steady even on the heights.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your viewpoint from the human to the divine, from the temporary to the eternal. Numbers are temporary; the God of my salvation is eternal. Change your thinking and your life changes: once the source of joy moves from results to God himself, pressure no longer defines me.
lessons.scene: Xiaohan started a pet food e-commerce business in Taipei three years ago and has eight staff. This afternoon, the investor who had agreed to fund them emails to say they are pulling out. There is only enough cash for two more months. She sits in the meeting room, about to address the whole team, with a forecast covered in red on the table, not knowing what her first sentence should be.
q: Who is God? — When Habakkuk says, ‘The LORD, the Lord, is my strength’, what kind of God does he know?
Who am I? — Is your joy usually built on ‘because’, or on ‘even though… yet’?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiaohan, how could she face the crisis honestly and still give her team hope?
lessons.jesus: To the disciples, the day of the cross was a dashboard of solid red: their Teacher arrested, crucified and buried, three years of following apparently wiped out. Yet on the third day the tomb was empty. Jesus’ resurrection tells us that in God’s hands, no red light is ever the final word.
lessons.pray: God of my salvation, you know the numbers and pressures I am facing. I confess my heart rises and falls with results, dragged along by spreadsheets. Be my strength, so that even when nothing flourishes I can still rejoice in you. Give me wisdom for the problems in front of me, and let the colleagues around me see hope in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before opening a report, pray Habakkuk 3:18 once
Write down three things that stay true about God even if results are poor
Speak one word of hope to a colleague under the same pressure
lessons.noon: “I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation” — Lord, right now I lift my eyes from the numbers to you.

lessons.title: Joy on Mains Power
lessons.theme: Happiness drains with circumstances, but joy flows from the Lord without ceasing

v: Always rejoice.
Pray without ceasing.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus towards you.

Then he said to them, “Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, for today is holy to our Lord. Don’t be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”

lessons.still: When you arrive at work, plug in your phone and watch the charging symbol light up. Say to the Lord, “Lord, my strength runs out too. Keep me connected to you all day, and let your joy be my strength.”
teach: After Nehemiah led the people in rebuilding the wall, Ezra read the law aloud. Hearing God’s word, the people remembered their sins and wept. Nehemiah told them, ‘Don’t be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.’ That joy did not ignore sin; it came after confession, from knowing that God still accepted them and was still with them. Paul likewise urged the Thessalonians, ‘Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks.’ The three belong together: the root of joy is unbroken connection with God.

Happiness is like your phone battery: full in the morning, then three meetings, fifty emails and one angry client later, it has dropped into the red. Joy is like the uninterruptible power supply in a server room: when the mains fail, it keeps the servers running, because it draws on another source. Happiness depends on what happens; joy depends on whom I am connected to. That is why Paul can say ‘always’ rejoice: that power source never cuts out.

‘Rejoice in the Lord always’: the key is ‘in the Lord’. The self-centred life tries to hold the day together by managing its own emotions, and grows ever more exhausted. The self-emptied life knows it is simply a vessel plugged into the source. Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself; the heart finds gladness, the head finds worry. You don’t have to fake happiness today, but you can choose to come back to the Lord again and again, and let his joy be your strength.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. Joy is fruit the Spirit bears, not an emotion I manufacture. Rely on the Spirit with your heart rather than on yourself with your head; when I stay connected to the Lord, joy becomes my strength at work.
lessons.scene: Wenbin is a hardware engineer at a drone company in Shenzhen. The new product launches next week; he has worked past midnight for three weeks straight, and tonight he finds the battery module overheating. At one in the morning, slumped in a lab chair with his phone at five per cent, a WeChat message from his mother pops up: “Son, are you happy these days?”
q: Who is God? — ‘The joy of the LORD is your strength.’ What does this show you about how God wants to supply you?
Who am I? — Today, is your heart more like a phone running down, or a power supply plugged into the mains?
How shall I respond? — If you were Wenbin, how could he answer his mother honestly and reconnect with God in his exhaustion?
lessons.jesus: On the night before the cross, Jesus told his disciples, “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full” (John 15:11). His joy did not come from easy circumstances but from perfect union with the Father. He gives us that joy so that we too may live connected to the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I often mistake happiness for joy, drawing near to you when I feel good and drifting away when I’m under pressure. Today help me keep returning to you, praying in the gaps between tasks and giving thanks in small things. My strength is limited; let your joy be my strength. And remind me to stop and rest when I need to, not to push on regardless. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Each time you charge your phone, thank the Lord in one sentence
Mark three small things to be thankful for on your task list
Take a proper lunch break today and give your body real rest
lessons.noon: “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks” — Lord, right now I plug into you again; fill me.

lessons.title: Grease in the Staffroom Air
lessons.theme: Complaining quietly stains a team, while thanksgiving makes people shine like lights

v: Do all things without complaining and arguing,
that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, amongst whom you are seen as lights in the world,
holding up the word of life, that I may have something to boast in the day of Christ that I didn’t run in vain nor labour in vain.

lessons.still: Before you enter the office, pause at the door and breathe deeply. Say to the Lord, “Lord, my lips belong to you today. When I want to complain, remind me to give thanks first.” Then walk in with a smile.
teach: Paul told the Philippians, ‘Do all things without complaining and arguing.’ The word for complaining recalls Israel grumbling all the way through the wilderness: the water was bitter, there was no meat, the manna was monotonous. Their bodies had left Egypt, but their hearts stayed stuck in complaint. Paul says those who do not grumble, in a crooked and perverse generation, ‘are seen as lights in the world’. In a world used to complaining, simply not complaining is a witness.

Complaining is like cooking grease in the air. At first you hardly notice; after enough frying, the walls, the ceiling and everyone’s clothes carry the smell. One line in the staffroom, ‘This place is hopeless’, soon clings to a whole team and makes everyone a little greyer. Thanksgiving is like the extractor fan above the hob, drawing the stale air away so people can breathe again. You don’t have to pretend everything is fine, but you can choose not to let complaint become the air the office breathes.

The root of complaining is often the self-centred life: I deserve better treatment, my ideas should be adopted, God should arrange things my way. Complaining is quietly a bid to be lord. Thanksgiving is a return to our proper place, confessing that everything is grace. Of course, not complaining doesn’t mean not speaking the truth. Problems should be raised through proper channels and with a constructive spirit. The difference: complaining dumps rubbish on others; honest feedback looks for a way forward together.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving one’s place to grasp power. Complaining is the heart wanting to be lord; thanksgiving lays power down, returns to its place and lets God be God. Pride provokes pride, and complaint breeds complaint; humility draws out humility, and one word of thanks draws out another.
lessons.scene: Grace teaches at a primary school in Auckland. Every lunchtime the staffroom fills with complaints: the new principal’s policies, parents’ emails, the ministry’s reviews. Today her colleague Mike starts again: “This school’s going to fall apart sooner or later.” Everyone looks at Grace, waiting for her to agree, her sandwich frozen halfway to her mouth.
q: Who is God? — Israel complained all through the wilderness, and God kept providing. What do you see of his patience?
Who am I? — In your workplace, are you more often the source of the ‘grease’, or the extractor fan?
How shall I respond? — If you were Grace, how could she decline to join in the complaining without making her colleagues feel judged?
lessons.jesus: Jesus endured misunderstanding, neglect and injustice all his life, yet he never grumbled. Scripture says, “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). He gave his grievances to the Father and his kindness to people. He is the brightest light in a crooked and perverse generation.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess my mouth often complains: about work, about my manager, about my circumstances, even about you. Forgive me and cleanse my lips. Today, when I want to grumble, let me see your grace first; when something is genuinely wrong, help me speak the truth in a fitting way. Make me a light in my workplace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: For every complaint you voice today, add one thank-you
Share one thing to be grateful for in the staffroom or break area
Turn one complaint into a specific, constructive suggestion
lessons.noon: “Do all things without complaining and arguing” — Lord, right now I hand you the thing I want to complain about.

lessons.title: The Office Thermostat
lessons.theme: Not merely reflecting the mood, but changing it with the Lord’s joy

v: A cheerful heart makes good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.
Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.

lessons.still: In the lift or on the stairs, place your hand on your chest and say, “God of hope, fill me with joy today, and let me carry your hope into the office.”
teach: Proverbs says, ‘A cheerful heart makes good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.’ The ancients already saw that the state of the heart affects the body and the people around us. Paul blesses the Roman church: ‘Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing.’ The source of joy is God, the channel is faith, and the result is that we ‘abound in hope’. A person filled with this joy is like an open bottle of perfume; the fragrance simply spreads.

A thermometer and a thermostat both hang on the wall, but they do very different jobs. A thermometer only reflects the room: if the office is cold, it reads cold; if the atmosphere is tense, so is the reading. A thermostat senses the temperature and then actively adjusts it, bringing the whole space back to comfort. Many Christians at work are thermometers, anxious and grumbling along with everyone else. God calls us to be thermostats, carrying his joy to change the temperature of a whole team.

This week we saw Paul rejoicing in chains, Habakkuk rejoicing under a dashboard of red, Nehemiah calling joy our strength, and we learned to replace complaint with thanks. Joy is not reserved for extroverts; it is fruit the Spirit bears in every believer. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: when your life is filled with the Lord’s joy, you become good medicine to your colleagues rather than another source of stress.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change works from the inside out, in five layers: thinking, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Joy is first filled into our life by God, then overflows into daily living, and finally becomes blessing in relationships. Of the ‘9’ fruits in 920, joy is the one colleagues feel most quickly.
lessons.scene: Xiaodong is the new manager of the claims department at an insurance company in Shanghai. At nine on Monday morning, the weekly meeting is heavy: complaints spiked last week, the system crashed again, and two people have handed in their notice. Xiaodong walks in holding a memo asking everyone to work overtime to catch up, and he can feel the temperature in the room drop to freezing.
q: Who is God? — Romans calls him ‘the God of hope’. What does that name mean for your situation today?
Who am I? — At work, are you more like a thermometer or a thermostat?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiaodong, what could he say or do before announcing the overtime, to give the team hope?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ first sign was turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana. The wine had run out and the celebration was about to fall flat, yet he made the master of the feast exclaim, “You have kept the good wine until now!” (John 2:10). Wherever Jesus goes, he brings renewal, hope and a better joy. He is willing to walk into your office today too.
lessons.pray: God of hope, fill my heart with joy and peace in believing. I don’t want simply to rise and fall with my surroundings, but to carry your joy into every meeting and every conversation. Today make me good medicine to my colleagues, bringing your hope to them through a word of encouragement, a smile and sincere thanks. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: In today’s meeting, begin by naming one thing the team did well
Thank a colleague in specific words
Before leaving, ask yourself: did I raise the office temperature today?
lessons.noon: “A cheerful heart makes good medicine” — Lord, right now let your joy flow out from my heart.

mem.t: And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.title: Raise a Ticket with God
lessons.theme: Hand every worry over to God, and let his peace stand guard over my heart

v: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Before work, write today’s biggest worry on a sticky note. Press it into your palm, close your hands over it and say, “Lord, I hand this over to you. Let your peace guard my heart.” Then put the note in your pocket.
teach: When Paul says, ‘In nothing be anxious’, he isn’t telling us to pretend all is well. He gives a concrete way out: ‘but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.’ ‘Everything’ covers the big things and the small; ‘thanksgiving’ reminds us that the God who was faithful yesterday will be faithful today. The result: ‘the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.’ ‘Guard’ is a military word, like a sentry posted at a city gate.

Many companies use a ticketing system for problems: spot an issue, raise a ticket, describe it clearly and assign it to the team responsible. Once it is raised, you don’t stare at it all night, because someone now owns it. Prayer is like raising a ticket for your worry and assigning it to the almighty Lord of heaven. The trouble is that many of us raise the ticket and then take it straight back to handle ourselves, praying and worrying at the same time. Real entrusting means believing the one who owns it is more reliable than you.

The root of worry is often ‘I must be in control’. The self-centred life tries to hold everything in its own hands, and the tighter it grips, the more afraid it becomes. Humility lays power down and returns to its place: I do my part and leave the outcome with God. This isn’t irresponsibility; it is knowing who is truly responsible. As we entrust things like this, the peace that ‘surpasses all understanding’ comes, not because the problem is solved, but because we know whose hands it is in.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying power down and returning to one’s place, letting God be God. Worry tries to be lord in God’s place; prayer hands authority back to him. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on circumstances: peace is not the absence of problems but a heart guarded in Christ.
lessons.scene: Wanting is an auditor at an accounting firm in Taipei. Tomorrow morning her manager will review the client file she is responsible for, and she has just found an inventory figure that doesn’t reconcile. Three hours of checking haven’t found the cause. At eleven at night she lies in bed, running every worst-case scenario, with a message from her manager on her phone: “See you at eight.”
q: Who is God? — God’s peace ‘surpasses all understanding’. What kind of guardian does this show him to be?
Who am I? — Do you often ‘raise the ticket and take it back’, praying and worrying at the same time?
How shall I respond? — If you were Wanting, how could she pray tonight, and how could she face her manager honestly tomorrow?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, Jesus was sorrowful to the point of death. He didn’t bury it; he fell on his face and prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). He brought his deepest anguish to the Father, then rose and walked calmly towards the cross.
lessons.pray: Father, I tell you my worries one by one: the deadlines, my manager’s opinion, the problems still unsolved. I confess I often want to control everything, and the tighter I hold on, the more afraid I become. Now I give these to you, and I thank you for your faithfulness in the past. Let your peace stand guard over my heart and my thoughts like a sentry. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down today’s three biggest worries and pray over each one
Beside each worry, write one thing you can thank God for
Do your part today, then tell yourself: the outcome is God’s
lessons.noon: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer” — Lord, right now I give this worry to you.

lessons.title: The Eye of the Storm
lessons.theme: With the Lord in the boat, no storm can sink it

v: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let’s go over to the other side.”
Leaving the multitude, they took him with them, even as he was, in the boat. Other small boats were also with him.
A big wind storm arose, and the waves beat into the boat, so much that the boat was already filled.
He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion; and they woke him up and asked him, “Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?”
He awoke and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The wind ceased and there was a great calm.
He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?”
They were greatly afraid and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”

lessons.still: Once you are on the bus or train, close your eyes and picture yourself in a boat with Jesus sitting beside you. Say softly, “Lord, you are in my boat. Whatever wind blows today, I will not be afraid.”
teach: ‘Let’s go over to the other side’ was Jesus’ own idea. The disciples obeyed and got into the boat, only to be hit by a violent storm. Waves broke over the side until the boat was filling. Several of these men were seasoned fishermen, and even they were terrified. Jesus, meanwhile, was ‘in the stern, asleep on the cushion’. They woke him: ‘Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?’ He rose and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’ and there was a great calm. Then he asked, ‘Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?’

The most dangerous part of a cyclone is the ring of wind around it, but at its very centre lies the eye, where the air is still and you can even see blue sky. Jesus asleep in the boat was like someone living in the eye of the storm: wind and rain outside, his heart at rest in the Father’s presence. Project delays, client pressure and redundancy rumours can all be the storm’s outer ring at work. But as long as the Lord is in the boat, we can be drawn into the eye.

Notice that the storm came after obedience. Doing what God says doesn’t guarantee smooth sailing. But God’s promise holds: if he says we are going to the other side, we will get there. The disciples’ problem was not the storm; it was forgetting who was in the boat. Change your thinking and your life changes: from ‘Lord, don’t you care?’ to ‘Lord, with you here, I am at peace.’ Peace is not the absence of storms; it is the Lord with us in the storm.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example. Sleeping through the storm, he showed a life of complete trust in the Father. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on circumstances; when my eyes move from the waves to the Lord in the boat, fear gives way to faith.
lessons.scene: Ethan is site manager for a construction company in Christchurch, building a new medical centre. Three weeks of heavy rain have put the project badly behind schedule, and this afternoon the client rang to threaten the penalty clause if there are any more delays. In the site office, the crew look at him, waiting for him to decide whether they work through the rain tomorrow.
q: Who is God? — The disciples asked, ‘Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?’ Is this the Jesus you know?
Who am I? — Facing storms at work, do you more often say ‘Don’t you care?’ or ‘With you here, I am at peace’?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ethan, how could he make a peaceful decision between safety, the schedule and the client’s pressure?
lessons.jesus: Jesus slept in the boat because he trusted the Father completely; he rebuked the wind because he is the Lord who made wind and sea. Later he faced a far greater storm, the cross, and still obeyed to the end. He is in the boat and in our lives. He calmed the waves, and he calmed the separation between us and God.
lessons.pray: Lord, you see the storms in my work: pressure, delays, an uncertain future. I confess I often panic like the disciples and ask whether you care. Let me see that you are right here in my boat, and draw me into your peace. Give me wisdom to make sound decisions, neither rash out of fear nor compromising on safety under pressure. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one ‘storm’ in your work and hand it to the Lord
Before any important decision, pray quietly for five minutes
Ask an anxious colleague, “Shall we pray about this together?”
lessons.noon: “Peace! Be still!” — Lord, right now calm the storm inside me.

lessons.title: The Earth Wire
lessons.theme: Peacemakers channel the high voltage of conflict into God’s peace

v: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

lessons.still: On the way to work, think of the tense relationships you may meet today. Open your hands and say to the Lord, “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace. Where there is conflict, let me carry your peace.”
teach: Jesus said, ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.’ He didn’t say peace-lovers but peacemakers: not avoiding conflict but stepping into it to bring reconciliation. James adds that the wisdom from above is ‘first pure, then peaceful’. Making peace is not papering over cracks; it rests on truth and righteousness. And he concludes, ‘the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.’

Every electrician knows the importance of the earth wire. When an appliance develops a fault, the earth wire carries the dangerous current safely into the ground so nobody gets a shock. Workplace conflict is like a fault current: two departments blaming each other, colleagues giving each other the silent treatment, and anyone who touches it gets a jolt. A peacemaker is like that earth wire. Not absorbing all the voltage, but channelling the conflict somewhere safe: to God, and to a space where people can talk honestly, so no one else gets hurt.

Making peace begins with our own peace with God. Someone without peace inside struggles to bring peace to others; the self-centred life, in conflict, only wants to prove itself right. Humility draws out humility: when I first admit my own blind spots, the other person finds it easier to lower their guard. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. That doesn’t make the task unimportant; it means that while we deal with the task, we don’t wound people.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility draws out humility (both win); pride provokes pride (both lose). Peacemakers lay down the need to win, return to their place and bring both sides back before God. This is how we build God’s order at work.
lessons.scene: Binghong is an HR officer at a food factory in Tainan. Production and quality control are blaming each other over a returned shipment; the two department heads haven’t spoken in two weeks, and their staff are taking sides. The owner has handed the matter to Binghong. Tomorrow at three he must bring both heads into the same meeting room, and he sits at his desk unsure what his opening sentence should be.
q: Who is God? — Jesus says peacemakers ‘shall be called children of God’. What kind of Father does this show God to be?
Who am I? — In workplace conflict, are you more often the one who avoids it, the one who takes sides, or the peacemaker?
How shall I respond? — If you were Binghong, how could he open the meeting so that both heads feel free to speak honestly?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the greatest peacemaker. Scripture says, “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation” (Ephesians 2:14). He didn’t urge peace from a distance; he bore the full weight of the conflict himself. On the cross he made it possible for people to be reconciled to God and to one another.
lessons.pray: Lord of peace, thank you for first making peace between me and you. Make me an instrument of peace at work, neither running from conflict nor adding fuel to the fire. When I face colleagues blaming one another, give me the wisdom from above, first pure, then peaceful. Help me deal with problems without wounding people. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray by name for one tense relationship between colleagues
Don’t pass on anything negative one side says about the other
Seek out a colleague you’ve drifted from and ask how they are
lessons.noon: “Blessed are the peacemakers” — Lord, right now make me an instrument of your peace.

lessons.title: The Meeting-Room Mixing Desk
lessons.theme: In a heated meeting, turn myself down first, then hear others

v: There was strife between the herdsmen of Abram’s livestock and the herdsmen of Lot’s livestock. The Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land at that time.
Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.
Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.”
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.still: Before you enter the meeting room, pause outside for three seconds. Place a hand on your chest and say, “Lord, today let me listen before I speak and answer gently. In this meeting I want you to be King.”
teach: The herdsmen of Abram and Lot were fighting over pasture and water. As the elder, Abram had the right to choose first; by promise, God had given him the land. Yet he said to Lot, ‘Please, let there be no strife between you and me… for we are relatives.’ He even let Lot choose: ‘If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right.’ Abram laid down his rights and gained peace in the relationship. Proverbs says, ‘A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.’

A recording studio has a mixing desk covered in faders, each controlling one track. A good sound engineer doesn’t push every fader to the top; he balances them so every voice can be heard. A conflicted meeting often sounds as if every fader is maxed out: everyone talking loudly, no one listening. Being a peacemaker means first pulling your own fader down a little, then bringing up the voice nobody has heard: ‘I’d like to hear what the design team thinks first.’

Abram gave way not out of weakness but because he trusted God. He knew God’s promise wouldn’t be lost by yielding. And after Lot left, God himself told him, ‘I will give all the land which you see to you.’ Humility isn’t losing; it is handing winning and losing to God. In a meeting you can state your professional view clearly, but you don’t need to make others feel defeated in order to prove yourself right.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is the key to revival. Abram laid down his rights, returned to his place and let God be God; he lost nothing and gained God’s promise. In meetings, humility draws out humility: one gentle answer can cool a whole room.
lessons.scene: Yongqi is marketing manager for a beauty brand in Singapore. In the product launch meeting, sales and design are locked in a fierce argument over packaging colours, and the sales director has just slammed the table. Everyone turns to Yongqi, because the final call is hers, and privately she already leans towards the sales team’s view.
q: Who is God? — Abram dared to let Lot choose first. What kind of God did he believe in?
Who am I? — In meetings, do you usually push your own fader to the top, or are you willing to turn it down first?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yongqi, how could she make both sides feel heard before she makes the final call?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper the disciples argued about who was greatest. Jesus didn’t join the argument; he said, “I am amongst you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). He is Lord of the universe, yet he willingly turned himself down so that we could be lifted up. His humility quieted their rivalry and showed us how to be peacemakers in conflict.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are King of kings, yet you were among your disciples as one who serves. Teach me in meetings to listen first and speak second, to answer gently and not harshly. When I want to prove myself right, remind me to hand winning and losing to you. In every meeting, make me a peacemaker. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: In today’s meeting, ask a quieter colleague for their view first
Before answering an objection, say, “What I hear you saying is…”
After the meeting, privately thank a colleague who disagreed with you
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath” — Lord, right now let my words carry your gentleness.

lessons.title: The Referee in My Heart
lessons.theme: Let God’s peace, the peace Christ gives, referee my choices

v: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.
Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.

lessons.still: Before you leave, sit quietly for a minute. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I have many decisions to make today. Let your peace rule in my heart, and when I drift from you, blow the whistle.”
teach: Paul writes, ‘let the peace of God rule in your hearts.’ The word translated ‘rule’ carries the idea of acting as an umpire, like the official who decides what is a foul and what is a goal. The peace Christ gives is the referee in our hearts: when we walk in God’s will, there is peace; when we drift, peace blows the whistle. Jesus himself said, ‘My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you.’

Modern football has the video assistant referee. When there is a contested moment, the referee can pause, review the footage and then rule. Workplace decisions have contested moments too: take this contract or not? Change jobs? Play down a figure in the report? The world’s peace is conditional: the pay is high enough, the risk low enough. Christ’s peace comes from our relationship with him. Before major decisions, press pause, come back to the Lord, and let his peace make the final call.

This week we learned to hand over our worries, trust in the storm, be peacemakers, and turn ourselves down in meetings. At the centre of it all is letting Jesus be King. When his peace rules our hearts, we are no longer dragged along by fear, greed or other people’s opinions. Paul goes on, ‘and be thankful’: gratitude reminds us that peace is grace, not a reward we have earned.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting Jesus be King includes letting his peace rule in my heart. The Holy Spirit is my guide: before important choices, rely on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. When the referee in my heart blows the whistle, being willing to stop is obedience.
lessons.scene: Aroha is a policy analyst in a government department in Wellington. Head office has offered her a management role in Auckland with thirty per cent more pay, but her parents are getting older and the youth ministry at her church has only just begun. She must answer by Monday. She has filled two pages with pros and cons, and the longer the list grows, the more unsettled her heart becomes.
q: Who is God? — Jesus says, ‘not as the world gives, I give to you.’ How is his peace different from the world’s?
Who am I? — In career decisions, do you more often follow the calculation of conditions, or the whistle of the referee within?
How shall I respond? — If you were Aroha, how could she let Christ’s peace rule over her decision?
lessons.jesus: Jesus spoke these words on the night he was betrayed; with the cross right before him, he left his peace with his disciples. After his resurrection, he stood among them and his first words were, “Peace be to you” (John 20:19). This peace was bought with the cross, a gift no circumstance can take away.
lessons.pray: Lord of peace, thank you for giving me your peace, not as the world gives. I face many choices today; let your peace rule in my heart. When I am pulled along by gain, fear or others’ opinions, blow the whistle and remind me. Keep me thankful, and in every decision let you be King. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pause and pray for one minute before any important decision today
Notice the moment you lose peace today, and note why
Before leaving work, write down three things to be thankful for
lessons.noon: “Let the peace of God rule in your hearts” — Lord, right now I hand this decision to you.

mem.t: Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

lessons.title: Trials in the Weights Room
lessons.theme: Trials are not meant to crush me but to train endurance in me

v: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations,
knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.
Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

lessons.still: When you get up, stretch your arms and feel the tightness in your muscles. Say to the Lord, “Lord, if trials come today, help me remember that you are training me, not abandoning me.”
teach: James opens startlingly: ‘Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations.’ The word also means trials. He isn’t asking us to enjoy suffering, but to know something: ‘the testing of your faith produces endurance.’ ‘Testing’ was the word for proving gold and silver in the fire to show their true quality. And he concludes, ‘Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.’ The destination of trials is not pain but maturity.

Anyone who has trained at a gym knows muscles don’t grow while you are comfortable. Lifting more than usual creates tiny tears in the muscle fibres; with rest, the body repairs them and the muscle comes back stronger. A coach will say, ‘Soreness is a sign you’re growing.’ Workplace trials are similar: the proposal sent back, the impossible project, the promotion postponed again. Each may be weight God has placed on us, to build a faith that can carry more.

‘Count it all joy’ asks for a change of viewpoint. From the human angle, trials are loss; from God’s angle, they are investment. Change your thinking and your life changes. The self-centred life in trials only asks, ‘Why me?’ The self-emptied life asks, ‘Lord, what do you want to accomplish in me through this?’ Endurance is not gritting your teeth; it is continuing to trust in the middle of the trial, giving God time to complete his work.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your viewpoint from the human to the divine, from the temporary to the eternal. People see trials as obstacles; God uses them as training. Among the eight steps, ‘repetition’ is exactly where endurance is built.
lessons.scene: Qihang is a product manager at a games studio in Chengdu. His proposal for a new game has just been sent back by senior management for the third time, with a different reason each time. When the rejection arrives this afternoon, colleagues in the team chat are already sharing CV templates. He stares at his screen, his finger hovering over a draft resignation letter.
q: Who is God? — James says the testing of faith ‘produces endurance’. How do you see God using trials to make you complete?
Who am I? — Facing trials at work, do you more often ask ‘Why me?’ or ‘Lord, what are you accomplishing?’
How shall I respond? — If you were Qihang, how could he seek God’s guidance before deciding whether to stay or go?
lessons.jesus: Jesus went through trials too, even the greatest trial of all, the cross. Scripture says that ‘for the joy that was set before him’ he ‘endured the cross, despising its shame’ (Hebrews 12:2). He saw salvation completed on the far side of the trial, and so he endured to the end. Today he walks with us in our trials.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I don’t like trials; I often just want to escape. But today I choose to believe you are training my faith through these difficulties. Give me strength to endure, not by gritting my teeth but by continuing to trust you. Let endurance have its perfect work in me, so that I may be complete. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one current trial, and beside it: God is training me
When a setback hits today, take three deep breaths before responding
Share your trial with a trusted believer and ask them to pray
lessons.noon: “The testing of your faith produces endurance” — Lord, right now I trust that you are training me.

lessons.title: Parcel in Transit
lessons.theme: Like a farmer waiting for harvest, I strengthen my heart in the unseen days

v: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.
You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.

lessons.still: Before you leave, hold a glass of water in both hands and drink slowly, picturing rain soaking into a field. Say to the Lord, “Lord, you send the early and late rain. Today I will wait for you patiently. Establish my heart.”
teach: James uses the farmer as his picture of patience: ‘the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.’ In Israel, the early rain fell around sowing time so the seed could sprout; the late rain fell before harvest to fill out the grain. The farmer did all he could: ploughing, sowing, weeding. What remained was waiting for God to send rain. He didn’t dig up the soil every day to check on the seed; he trusted that in time there would be a harvest.

Anyone who shops online knows one status well: ‘In transit’. You have ordered and paid, but the parcel hasn’t arrived. You can check the tracking ten times a day, and it won’t arrive any faster. Many people changing jobs, looking for work or waiting for promotion live in that ‘in transit’ state: CVs sent, interviews done, and still no answer. James says, ‘You also be patient. Establish your hearts.’ Waiting days are not wasted days; they are days for roots to grow deep.

Patient waiting isn’t passively doing nothing. Like the farmer, we do our part and leave the outcome with God. The self-centred life wants to control the timetable and, unable to wait, grabs things for itself; the self-emptied life trusts that God’s timing is best. James says ‘the coming of the Lord is at hand’; from eternity’s perspective, all our waiting today is temporary. So in the waiting, let’s keep sowing, keep praying and keep trusting.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Turn from the temporary to the eternal. The farmer’s patience rests on trust in the God who sends rain; ours rests on faith in the Lord. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on the timetable.
lessons.scene: Shuwei was made redundant by a tech company in Kaohsiung eight months ago. Since then he has sent out more than forty applications and had six interviews, none of which led anywhere. This morning another email arrives: “Thank you for your application.” His wife pats his shoulder as she leaves for work. He sits at the computer, unsure whether to send the next one.
q: Who is God? — James says God sends ‘the early and late rain’. What does this show you of God’s timing?
Who am I? — In your own ‘in transit’ season, do you keep checking the tracking, or do your part and rest in God?
How shall I respond? — If you were Shuwei, what seeds could he sow while he waits, and who could walk with him?
lessons.jesus: Scripture says Jesus ‘was about thirty years old’ when he began his public ministry (Luke 3:23), and it tells us little about the years before. He was the Son of God, yet he waited for the Father’s appointed time before stepping into public service. His patience was not passive waiting but rest within the Father’s timetable.
lessons.pray: Lord, you know the anxiety and weariness of my waiting. I confess I often want to control the timetable, and lose heart when I can’t wait any longer. Establish my heart, so that like the farmer I do my part and patiently wait for your early and late rain. And in these waiting days, let me not be alone or give up, but have brothers and sisters walking with me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Sow one seed today: learn a skill or contact someone
Limit how many times you check for results today
Pray for a friend who is also waiting
lessons.noon: “You also be patient. Establish your hearts” — Lord, right now in my waiting I give my heart to you.

lessons.title: Don’t Pick Unripe Fruit
lessons.theme: The place God has promised need not be seized by my own hand

v: David’s men said to him, “Behold, the day of which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.’” Then David arose and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe secretly.
Afterward, David’s heart struck him because he had cut off Saul’s skirt.
He said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed.”
So David checked his men with these words, and didn’t allow them to rise against Saul. Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.

lessons.still: Before work, clench your hands gently, then slowly open them. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I let go of the hands that want to grab for myself, and I give my future to you. Today, let me take no shortcuts, only your way.”
teach: David was anointed by Samuel as a young man, but only after many years on the run from Saul did he actually take the throne. In a cave at En Gedi, the chance came: Saul walked in alone, and David’s men said, ‘Behold, the day of which the LORD said to you…’ David only secretly cut off the edge of Saul’s robe, and afterwards ‘David’s heart struck him’. He said, ‘The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed.’ David trusted that what God had promised, God would fulfil in his time, without David having to seize it.

Kitchens have microwaves and slow cookers. A microwave heats food in three minutes, but the meat often comes out dry and tough; a slow cooker takes hours, yet the meat is tender and full of flavour. At work, people often urge the microwave method: get something on the boss, stab a rival in the back, climb over others to get ahead. David chose the slow cooker: better to wait for God’s time than to grab what God had promised by unrighteous means.

David’s patience was not weakness but the fear of God. He knew judgement belonged to God, not to him; he returned to his place and let God be God. The self-centred life wants to be lord and reaches out its hand when God seems slow; the self-emptied life trusts God to fulfil his promise in his own time. The days of patient waiting are the days God shapes our character, preparing us for the place he means to entrust to us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving one’s place to grasp power; humility is laying power down and returning to one’s place. David held the knife but chose not to strike. That is returning to his place and letting God be God. The place God intends to entrust will come in his time.
lessons.scene: Darren Lim is assistant manager at a logistics firm in Johor Bahru. His warehouse improvement plan was presented to head office by his manager as the manager’s own work. A colleague privately sends Darren a screenshot of an abusive personal message the manager wrote: “Forward this to HQ and he’s finished. The job’s yours.” Darren stares at the screenshot, his finger hovering over ‘Forward’.
q: Who is God? — David trusted God to fulfil his promise in his time. Do you believe God is that faithful?
Who am I? — At work, have you ever been tempted to use the ‘microwave method’ to seize what you felt you deserved?
How shall I respond? — If you were Darren, how should he handle the stolen credit, and what should he do with that screenshot?
lessons.jesus: In the wilderness, the devil took Jesus to a very high mountain, showed him the glory of all the kingdoms, and said, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9).
