It was a shortcut that bypassed the cross. Jesus refused it and chose the Father’s way: suffering first, then glory. Now he is seated at the Father’s right hand, and every knee will bow to him.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I sometimes want to fight for myself, settle my own scores, even use wrong means to get what I want. Forgive me, and help me, like David, to fear you and not stretch out my hand to do wrong. I give you my future and my grievances. Where it is needed, give me wisdom to speak the truth through proper means. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one thing you want to grab for yourself, and entrust it to God
Speak badly of no one behind their back today
If you face unfairness, think how to raise it through proper channels
lessons.noon: “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord” — Lord, right now I let go of the urge to take matters into my own hands.

lessons.title: The Flavour of the Old Broth
lessons.theme: Keep doing good through repetition and difficult people; the Lord makes no labour vain

v: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

lessons.still: As you sit down, before putting on your headset, say to the Lord, “Lord, today I face the same work and the same people again. Help me remember that my labour is not in vain in you.”
teach: Paul told the Galatians, ‘Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.’ And the Corinthians: ‘be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.’ Both passages admit that doing good wears us out, and both promise an outcome: ‘we will reap in due season’, ‘not in vain’. Endurance doesn’t persevere because it has seen the result; it perseveres because it believes in the result.

Old family-run braised-meat shops in Asia keep a master stock: a pot of broth topped up and simmered every day, some for decades. Customers say, ‘You can’t find this flavour anywhere else.’ That flavour wasn’t made in a day; it came from countless ordinary days. A call-centre agent answers the same questions daily and faces difficult customers, as if starting over each morning. But in God’s eyes, every act of patience and every gentle answer is slowly simmering a life of rare and rich flavour.

‘Always abounding in the Lord’s work’: for many Christians, the daily round at work is the Lord’s work. When you offer repetitive tasks to the Lord, they stop being mere routine. The self-centred life sees only boredom in repetition; the self-emptied life sees that every person is loved by God. People matter more than tasks: behind a difficult customer there may be a weary person who needs gentleness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; never wound someone for the sake of a task. 920 reminds me that everyone connected to me is my ‘2’, including the difficult customer on the other end of the line. Enduring through repetition is letting the Spirit bear the fruit of patience.
lessons.scene: Peishan works in the call centre of a telecoms company in Taichung, taking eighty calls a day. This afternoon an elderly man rings for the fifth time about the same bill, shouting at her every time. Her supervisor has reminded her to keep call times down. She looks at the number flashing on her screen and takes a deep breath.
q: Who is God? — God promises that ‘we will reap in due season’. What does this show you of how he sees your ordinary labour?
Who am I? — Faced with repetitive work and difficult people, do you mostly feel bored and irritated, or do you see God’s purpose?
How shall I respond? — If you were Peishan, how could she balance keeping the call short with treating the elderly man gently?
lessons.jesus: In his three years of ministry, Jesus faced the same questions and the same lack of understanding again and again. The disciples argued about who was greatest and kept missing his teaching; the crowds pressed in, many only to be fed. Yet Jesus did not give up. He taught, healed and forgave, time after time. His patience is the ground we stand on today.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that in repetitive work and with difficult people I often lose heart and grow impatient. Renew my sight, so that I see every call and every customer as someone you love. Give me strength to endure, not to grow weary or give up, trusting that my labour is not in vain in you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before taking a difficult customer’s call, pray one line for them
Do one repetitive task with more care than yesterday
Before leaving work, thank God that today’s labour was not in vain
lessons.noon: “Let’s not be weary in doing good” — Lord, right now give me strength to endure.

lessons.title: Printed Layer by Layer
lessons.theme: God who began a good work will complete it; endurance lets him finish

v: being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.
Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance;
and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope;

lessons.still: Before the school run, or as you begin the day’s housework, cross your hands over your chest. Say to the Lord, “Lord, you have begun a good work in me, and you will complete it. Today I choose to trust your timetable.”
teach: From prison Paul wrote to the Philippians, ‘being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.’ To the Romans he wrote, ‘we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope.’ This is a chain of growth: suffering is not the end but the beginning; perseverance is not passive waiting but letting God finish his work in us.

A 3D printer works in an unusual way. It doesn’t produce the whole object at once, but builds it up layer by layer. Partway through, you often can’t tell what it is making: just a base and some untidy lines. But the design file already exists, and every layer moves towards the finished shape. God’s work in our lives is like that. We see only today’s layer, but he holds the complete design.

This week we learned to rejoice in trials, to wait like the farmer, not to pick unripe fruit, and to keep doing good through repetition. Today, remember: endurance having its perfect work is not the product of our own effort, but God completing his work. Success is not proof, and failure is not condemnation. Let’s keep trusting him layer by layer, let God be God, and let Jesus receive all the glory, because he will complete it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. The fruit of endurance is not my achievement but God’s workmanship. Among the eight steps, ‘repetition’ is where God completes his work layer by layer; all we need to do is keep trusting.
lessons.scene: Pei’en is a stay-at-home mother in Kuala Lumpur. For five years she has cared for two children and her father-in-law, who had a stroke: cooking, washing, school runs, medicines, day after day. Tonight, with the children asleep, she sits at the kitchen table reading her sister’s news of a promotion, and can’t help asking, “What have I actually achieved all these years?”
q: Who is God? — Paul is confident that God ‘will complete it’. Do you believe God finishes what he starts?
Who am I? — In days when you see no results, do you also ask, ‘What have I actually achieved?’
How shall I respond? — If you were Pei’en, how could she see in ordinary housework the work God is completing layer by layer?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished!” (John 19:30). He didn’t give up halfway; he completed the work the Father had given him. The Lord who completed salvation on the cross will also complete the good work he has begun in us. Our endurance rests on his finished work.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that you have begun a good work in me and will complete it. I confess that when I can’t see results, I lose heart and doubt. Help me trust that you hold the complete design, and keep me enduring and trusting through every ordinary day. Complete your work in me, and let Jesus receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one thing God has completed in you over the past year
Offer thanks to God over one repetitive chore or task
Ask family to cover an hour of caregiving so you can rest
lessons.noon: “He who began a good work in you will complete it” — Lord, right now I give you what is still unfinished.

mem.t: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: Oil Between the Gears
lessons.theme: Kindness is not weakness; it keeps a team from wearing itself down

v: Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.still: Sit down and rest your open hands on your knees, as if slowly unclenching a fist. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I put yesterday’s bitterness and resentment into your hands. Today, let me treat people with the kindness you have shown me.”
teach: In Ephesians 4 Paul writes a ‘put away’ list: “all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander… with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). They work like a chain reaction. Bitterness settles in the heart, ferments into wrath and anger, and finally bursts out of the mouth as outcry and slander. But Paul does not only tell us what to remove; he tells us what to put in its place: “be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other.” And the measure is breathtaking: “just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).

On a factory floor, a machine’s gears will keep turning even without oil. But every turn grinds metal on metal; heat builds, wear spreads, and one day the line seizes up. Teams are the same. Without kindness, projects still move and reports still get filed, but every day there is friction: a barbed reply, a rolled eye, a sigh in the meeting. Kindness is the thin film of oil nobody sees, and it is what lets the whole line keep running for years.

The source of kindness is not our good temper but God’s kindness to us first. When I remember that I owed a debt I could never repay, and that in Christ it has been cancelled, it becomes very hard to keep gripping a colleague’s small mistake. This is change from the inside out: my thinking changes first — ‘I am someone who has received grace’; then my life softens; then my tone, my face and my messages change too. Kindness is not a personality type. It is fruit the Holy Spirit grows in us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Don’t wound a person over a rework order. Every colleague around me is one of my ‘2’ — and the Spirit wants to grow the fruit of kindness in me in front of them. That is 920 at work: in every ‘2’, a self-emptied ‘0’ bearing the nine fruits of the Spirit.
lessons.scene: Jiaying is a production-line supervisor at an electronics factory. This morning she discovered that a new operator had labelled a whole batch of circuit boards with the wrong part numbers. Everything has to be reworked, and the team faces two extra hours tonight. In the thirty-person line group chat, she has already typed: “Is anyone actually paying attention? How many times do I have to say it?” Her thumb hovers over Send.
q: Who is God? — “Just as God also in Christ forgave you”: what does this show you about how God treats your mistakes?
Who am I? — Of the things Paul tells us to put away, which one shows up most often in your work?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jiaying, how would you rewrite that message so it deals with the problem and still carries a tender heart?
lessons.jesus: Peter denied Jesus three times. After the resurrection, Jesus did not humiliate him in front of everyone. He lit a charcoal fire on the beach, made breakfast, and then asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). Jesus deals with failure by leading with kindness, and only then entrusting a mission. We can be kind because we have first been treated this way.
lessons.pray: Kind Lord, in Christ you have forgiven my every debt, yet I so often hold on to a colleague’s small mistake. Take away the bitterness and resentment in my heart, and guard my fingers as I type in the group chat. When I meet someone who has slipped up today, let me show compassion first and solve the problem second, so that people taste your kindness in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before sending any rebuke, delete one barbed word
Privately tell a colleague who erred: “Let’s fix it together”
Before leaving, thank God for one kindness he has shown you
lessons.noon: “Be kind to one another, tender hearted” — Lord, right now I hand you the harsh words I want to say, and take up your gentleness instead.

lessons.title: The New Manager’s Table
lessons.theme: Kindness goes looking for someone to bless

v: David said, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
There was of Saul’s house a servant whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David; and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
The king said, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”
Then King David sent and brought him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar.
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face, and showed respect. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He answered, “Behold, your servant!”

David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate continually at the king’s table. He was lame in both his feet.

lessons.still: Before work, close your eyes and picture a face you would rather not see today. You don’t have to force yourself to like them. Just say: “Lord, as you have been kind to me, let me show your kindness to them.” Then breathe deeply and go.
teach: Once David was secure on the throne, his question was not ‘Who still threatens my crown?’ but “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?” (2 Samuel 9:1). In the ancient world, a new king often wiped out the old dynasty. Mephibosheth was Saul’s grandson, lame in both feet, living in someone else’s house in Lo Debar. When he was summoned, he fell on his face — perhaps expecting the worst. David’s first words were “Don’t be afraid.” Then he restored the family land and said, “You will eat bread at my table continually” (2 Samuel 9:7).

It is rather like a new manager arriving. On the desk lies a list of the previous boss’s people. Everyone knows who belongs to ‘the old regime’. A reorganisation is the perfect chance to move them on and enjoy some peace and quiet. David turned the list around. He was not looking for who should go, but for whom he could bless. He turned a purge list into a seating plan for his own table. Kindness is not merely saying yes when someone asks; it goes looking for the person hiding in the corner who thinks there is no place for them.

David said he wanted to “show the kindness of God” (2 Samuel 9:3). This was not political cunning; he was passing on the kindness he himself had received from God. Here is the turn from the self-centred life to the self-emptied life. The self-centred person asks, ‘Who is useful to me? Who threatens me?’ The self-emptied person asks, ‘For whose sake can I show kindness, and to whom?’ When we stop clutching our own position, there is room to save someone else a seat.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our proper place to grab power; humility is laying power down and returning to our place. David held great power, yet used it to show kindness rather than to protect himself. A manager who lets Jesus be King turns authority into a place of service.
lessons.scene: Junhong has just been promoted to head of marketing. One senior planner in the department was the previous manager’s favourite, and last month she openly opposed his proposal in a meeting. This week HR wants his restructuring chart. All he has to do is drag her name into another department’s column, and meetings will be quiet from now on. His cursor rests on her name.
q: Who is God? — David wanted to show “the kindness of God”. How has God taken the initiative to show kindness to you?
Who am I? — In your workplace, who is like Mephibosheth, tucked away in a corner, sure there is no place for them?
How shall I respond? — If you were Junhong, how would you draw up that chart in a way that shows the kindness of God?
lessons.jesus: We are all Mephibosheth: crippled by sin, hiding far away, convinced that a summons from the King can only mean judgement. Yet Jesus, for the sake of the covenant the Father made, came looking for us. He tells us not to be afraid and seats us at his table “like one of the king’s sons” (2 Samuel 9:11). Our legs are still weak, but every day he keeps a place for us at his table.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you that while I was hiding, you came looking for me and gave me a seat at your table. Make me someone who goes looking for people to bless. Today at work, open my eyes to the colleague who is overlooked, pushed out, or who once opposed me. Keep me from using my position to protect myself, and help me treat them with your kindness. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Invite a colleague you rarely talk to for lunch
In a meeting, affirm an often-overlooked person’s idea
Pray for a minute for someone who once opposed you
lessons.noon: “That I may show the kindness of God to him” — Lord, right now help me see the person near me who needs kindness.

lessons.title: Called by Name
lessons.theme: Jesus’ kindness comes before a person changes

v: He entered and was passing through Jericho.
There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
He was trying to see who Jesus was, and couldn’t because of the crowd, because he was short.
He ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was going to pass that way.
When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

lessons.still: Before you step out of the door, be still for ten seconds and imagine the Lord calling your name. Say to him: “Lord, you know me and you accept me. Today I don’t need to climb anywhere to prove myself. I just want to welcome you joyfully.”
teach: Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector in Jericho. He collected taxes for Rome, and he was rich — in his neighbours’ eyes, the very picture of a man who had sold out his own people. He was short and couldn’t see over the crowd, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree. When Jesus reached the spot, “he looked up and saw him,” and called him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). The crowd muttered. But Jesus did not demand repentance before he would come in. He came in first, and only then did Zacchaeus stand up and promise to give half his goods to the poor and repay four times over.

Many customer-service systems have a field called ‘problem customer’. Once someone has been flagged, the next agent sees that red label and their tone cools before they even say hello. People at work get labelled too: ‘the difficult one’, ‘the one who sucks up to the boss’, ‘the one who sells by smooth talk’. When Jesus walked into Jericho, everyone was holding a red label for Zacchaeus. Jesus looked past it and called him by name. Kindness is being willing to see the person under the label.

Zacchaeus was not scolded into change; he was loved into it. Jesus said, “The Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). He sought, he came in, and the man was changed from within. This is the 321 order: change your thinking and your life changes; change your life and your living changes. Zacchaeus first experienced acceptance, and only then gladly let go of his money. With difficult colleagues, we too can offer kindness first and leave the work of changing hearts to the Holy Spirit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on the labels on other people. I cannot change anyone, but like Jesus I can reach out with kindness first. Changing lives is the Spirit’s work; my part is to let Jesus be King and let his likeness live through me.
lessons.scene: Melissa leads a sales team at an insurance company in Kuala Lumpur. Zhenbang, on her team, has impressive numbers but is often accused of pushing sales with slick talk; behind his back colleagues call him ‘the old fox’. Today a client filed a complaint against him. For the first time he comes to Melissa’s desk and quietly asks if he could buy her lunch and talk. A few colleagues nearby are already exchanging looks.
q: Who is God? — Jesus called Zacchaeus by name while the crowd muttered. What kind of Lord does this show you?
Who am I? — Have you quietly stuck a ‘red label’ on a colleague?
How shall I respond? — If you were Melissa, with everyone watching, how would you respond to Zhenbang’s invitation?
lessons.jesus: People grumbled, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.” Jesus was willing to let his reputation suffer so that he could walk into the home of a lost man. On the cross he was even numbered among criminals. His kindness was costly: he carried the reputation of sinners so that sinners could carry his name.
lessons.pray: Lord who seeks the lost, thank you that while I was still hiding in the tree, you called my name. Peel off the labels I have stuck on my colleagues, and help me see that they too are people you are seeking. If someone comes to me for help today, keep me from fearing what others think. Let me offer kindness first and leave the changing to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Greet a colleague you’ve labelled, using their name
When others gossip about a colleague, add nothing
Pray for a colleague who is under complaint or left out
lessons.noon: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” — Lord, right now let me see the people around me through your eyes.

lessons.title: Boaz’s Onboarding List
lessons.theme: Kindness thinks of the next step for the weakest person

v: Then Boaz said to Ruth, “Listen, my daughter. Don’t go to glean in another field, and don’t go from here, but stay here close to my maidens.

Let your eyes be on the field that they reap, and go after them. Haven’t I commanded the young men not to touch you? When you are thirsty, go to the vessels, and drink from that which the young men have drawn.”
Then she fell on her face and bowed herself to the ground, and said to him, “Why have I found favour in your sight, that you should take knowledge of me, since I am a foreigner?”

Boaz answered her, “I have been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, and how you have left your father, your mother, and the land of your birth, and have come to a people that you didn’t know before.
May the LORD repay your work, and a full reward be given to you from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”

lessons.still: Before you clock in, think about who in your workplace is the newest, the quietest, the easiest to overlook. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you are the God who cares for the stranger. Today let me be a cup of water for someone who is thirsty.”
teach: Ruth was a Moabite: a foreigner, a widow and poor — on the edge three times over. She went to glean in the fields of Bethlehem. The law protected the right of the poor to do this, but it was also the work in which a person was most easily mistreated. Boaz, the owner, saw her and gave clear instructions: don’t go to another field; stay close to my young women; “Haven’t I commanded the young men not to touch you?”; and when you are thirsty, drink from the water the men have drawn (Ruth 2:8–9). Ruth was astonished: “Why have I found favour in your sight, that you should take knowledge of me, since I am a foreigner?” (Ruth 2:10).

Look closely and you will see that Boaz handed her an onboarding checklist: where you work, whom you work with, what protection you have, and where the water is. Good managers and experienced colleagues think of these things before the new person has to ask. Many new hires leave not because the job is too hard, but because in their first week nobody showed them how to log in, whom to have lunch with, or whom to ask when something goes wrong. A thoughtful onboarding list is kindness you can see.

Boaz’s kindness had roots. He knew that Ruth had come to the LORD, the God of Israel, “under whose wings you have come to take refuge” (Ruth 2:12). Boaz stretched out his own hand from under God’s wings. That is what it means to build God’s order: not one or two moments of enthusiasm, but making the protection of the vulnerable part of a team’s culture and processes. When the weakest people in a workplace can work in safety, the shape of God’s kingdom becomes visible on earth.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks. New hires, colleagues from abroad, temporary staff — each is a ‘2’ God has placed beside me. Catching them with kindness is how we build a godly system, so that Jesus receives the glory even in the least of these.
lessons.scene: Yuzhen is a senior nurse at a hospital in Taichung. This week a newly licensed nurse from Vietnam joined the ward. At handover she often can’t follow everyone’s spoken shorthand, and a senior colleague sighed at her in front of others. Today at lunch, Yuzhen sees her eating alone in a corner of the nurses’ station, flipping through her notes. Yuzhen had planned to use this half hour for a nap.
q: Who is God? — Boaz said Ruth had taken refuge under the wings of the God of Israel. How does this God see the vulnerable at work?
Who am I? — When you started your first job, who made a ‘Boaz list’ for you?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yuzhen, how would you use that half hour?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself became one of the marginalised: born in a manger, raised in despised Nazareth, rejected by his own people. Throughout his life he moved towards lepers, women, children and tax collectors. He became our true Redeemer — not just letting us glean a few ears of grain, but giving us his whole self.
lessons.pray: God who cares for the stranger, thank you for bringing me, an outsider, into your family. Today open my eyes to the newest, quietest person at work, the one who can’t keep up. Give me patience to share what I know, and courage to speak up for them when others sigh. Let them find in me the shelter of your wings. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Tell a new colleague one important thing no one taught
Invite someone eating alone for lunch or coffee
When someone sighs at another, add a softening word
lessons.noon: “Why have I found favour in your sight, that you should take knowledge of me” — Lord, right now let me take knowledge of the people around me like that.

lessons.title: A Charging Cable of Words
lessons.theme: One kind word can carry someone through a whole day

v: Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad.
Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.

lessons.still: Before you leave home, decide on one kind thing you will say to someone today and repeat it once in your heart. Then say to the Lord: “Lord, today take charge of my lips. Let my words be sweet like a honeycomb.”
teach: Proverbs says, “Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad” (Proverbs 12:25). Anxiety bends a person over; they shrink and stoop. What lifts them is sometimes not a long conversation but a single kind word. Proverbs adds, “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones” (Proverbs 16:24). In the ancient world honey was the most precious sweetness there was. The wise man says one good word carries that kind of weight: sweet enough to reach the soul, strong enough to heal the bones.

When your phone is down to five per cent, a charging cable is worth more than anything. Plenty of people arrive at work in exactly that state: a child with a fever last night, a complaint first thing this morning, a project stuck. Their battery is down to one bar. In that moment, a simple “Thanks for your hard work,” “Thank you for helping me,” or “You handled that really well” is a charging cable. It won’t solve every problem, but it may keep someone going until home time — until God opens the way for them.

Kind words are not flattery or empty politeness. They come from a heart filled with God’s kindness. When we ourselves are recharged daily by the Lord’s word, we have charge to spare for others. The self-centred person only notices how others treat them; the self-emptied person notices whose battery is running low today. This week we have seen kindness in David, in Jesus, in Boaz. Today, let it land in one sentence that comes out of your mouth.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use your heart and lean on the Spirit, not your head and your own strength. A kind word needn’t be crafted; it only needs eyes that truly see people. Saying one kind word each day to one of your ‘2’ is the simplest practice of 920 — the self-emptied life bearing fruit through the mouth.
lessons.scene: Ah Seng runs a long-established coffee shop in Penang. At eight in the morning, the busiest hour, the new teenage helper loses his grip and a whole tray of coffee cups smashes on the floor. Every customer turns to look. The boy goes pale, crouches down to pick up the pieces, and doesn’t dare look up. A sharp word is already rising in Ah Seng’s throat.
q: Who is God? — God says pleasant words bring “health to the bones”. What does this tell you about how much he values our words?
Who am I? — Has a recent word recharged you? Who said it?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ah Seng, what one sentence would you say to that boy?
lessons.jesus: The woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years secretly touched Jesus’ clothes and, when found out, came trembling. Jesus did not scold her. He called her “Daughter” and said, “Your faith has made you well. Go in peace” (Mark 5:34). With a few words he brought a woman shut out for years back into the community. Jesus’ words are the pleasant words that heal the bones.
lessons.pray: Lord, your words heal me and lift me up every day. Let my lips be a blessing to others today. Give me eyes to see who is close to running out, and courage to say, “Thank you for your hard work.” When I want to snap or be sarcastic, let your Spirit stop me, and let my words be sweet like a honeycomb. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Give one colleague a specific thank-you today
Send an encouraging message to someone who’s struggling
When you want to snap, take three breaths first
lessons.noon: “A kind word makes it glad” — Lord, right now let me speak a word that brings someone gladness.

mem.t: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we dont give up.

lessons.title: Curing Concrete
lessons.theme: Good that shows no results yet is still gaining strength

v: Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.
For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good towards all men, and especially towards those who are of the household of the faith.

lessons.still: Before you go, look down at your shoes and think: today I walk into the same place and face the same people again. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I’m a little tired. Give me fresh strength not to give up today, and help me sow to the Spirit.”
teach: Paul borrows a farmer’s logic: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7). Sow to the flesh and you reap corruption; sow to the Spirit and you reap eternal life. Then comes this week’s memory verse: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9). Notice the two kinds of time. “If we don’t give up” is our present; “in due season” is God’s time. Between sowing and reaping there is always a stretch of days with nothing to do but wait.

Anyone who works on a building site knows that once concrete has been poured, the critical stage is curing. You keep it wet, keep it covered, keep it moist — often for weeks — while its strength slowly develops. On the surface nothing seems to change, but skip that stage and the wall will crack. Doing good at work has a curing period too. You patiently answer the new hire again, deliver on time again, refuse to join the grumbling again. It looks as though nobody notices, but the strength of your character is quietly setting inside.

We lose heart when our focus drifts to the harvest. Has the person changed? Has the boss noticed? Will my appraisal show it? Paul pulls our focus back to the sower and the God who gives the harvest: “as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good towards all men” (Galatians 6:10). Our part is sowing; God’s part is the seasons. This is a shift in perspective from the temporary to the eternal. Today’s good is not an investment chasing a return; it is seed sown to the Spirit, into eternity.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Among the eight steps for changing our thinking is ‘repetition’. A changed life is not one burst of enthusiasm but practice repeated day after day. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on results; success proves nothing, and not yet seeing results is not failure.
lessons.scene: Ruoyu teaches at a primary school in New Taipei. All term she has stayed behind every Tuesday after school to help a boy in her class with homework — a boy who fights and never hands anything in. He has never said thank you, and yesterday he scribbled all over his contact book. This afternoon a colleague invited her to a Tuesday yoga class. Looking at her calendar, she wonders whether to cancel this week’s session.
q: Who is God? — “We will reap in due season”: what does this show you about how God rules the seasons?
Who am I? — In which act of goodness are you right now in a ‘curing period’ with no visible results?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ruoyu, how would you decide? Where is doing good, and where is the boundary of needed rest?
lessons.jesus: For three years Jesus sowed into his disciples. They often misunderstood, argued about who was greatest, and in the end scattered and ran. He did not lose heart; “he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). On the day of Pentecost the seed finally sprang up. We can keep going today because the Lord who never gave up is still at work in us.
lessons.pray: Lord of the harvest, you know I am a bit worn out. My efforts seem to vanish without a trace, and my kindness seems to go unnoticed. Remind me that sowing is my part and the seasons are yours. Give me new strength today to keep sowing to the Spirit in small things, and wisdom to know when I need to rest. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Keep doing one small good thing you wanted to quit
Note one small change from a seed you sowed earlier
Take a quiet rest today without guilt
lessons.noon: “We will reap in due season if we don’t give up” — Lord, right now I place the results I can’t see into your hands.

lessons.title: Clothes That Speak
lessons.theme: When someone is gone, the good she did still speaks for her

v: Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.
In those days, she became sick and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them.

Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
He gave her his hand and raised her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
This became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.

lessons.still: Pick up the tool you use most at work — a pen, a keyboard, a wok spatula, a steering wheel — and hold it. Say to the Lord: “Lord, what can these hands do for someone today? Please use whatever is in my hands.”
teach: Dorcas was a disciple in Joppa, and Scripture introduces her in a single line: “This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did” (Acts 9:36). When she died, the widows stood around Peter weeping, “showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them” (Acts 9:39). We can imagine that every stitch held her time and her love. She did not preach and worked no miracles, yet with needle and thread she left her mark on people in great need. God raised her through Peter, and “many believed in the Lord” (Acts 9:42).

Every office has a shared printer, and every office has someone who quietly refills the paper. People grumble when the paper runs out mid-job, but hardly anyone notices that the tray is usually full because someone keeps topping it up. Dorcas was the one who refilled the paper. Her goodness wasn’t in the spotlight; it soaked into the everyday lives of a whole group of people, until she was gone and everyone realised what was missing. The small things you do that make other people’s work go smoothly — those are the tunics you have sewn.

In the end Dorcas’s good works became a doorway for the gospel. This is the 321 order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Her life was captured by the Lord; her relationships with the widows grew deep through her kindness; and through those relationships God opened a door for ministry. We don’t have to wait for a title or a pulpit to bear witness to Christ. With the tools in your hands today, you can sew a garment that helps someone see him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Dorcas’s good works were not an evangelism strategy; they were fruit flowing naturally from a self-emptied life. And that is exactly the kind of fruit God loves to use to open people’s hearts.
lessons.scene: Mingzhe is an equipment engineer at a semiconductor company in Hsinchu. For three years he has quietly maintained a shared troubleshooting guide that every new hire relies on. At today’s performance review his manager said, “The time you spend on that document doesn’t count towards your KPIs. Cut back on it.” Back at his desk, Mingzhe opens the document. His cursor sits on a new entry he hasn’t finished.
q: Who is God? — God raised Dorcas and used it to bring many to faith. What does this show you about how he values ordinary goodness?
Who am I? — What ‘tunics and garments’ have your hands made at work?
How shall I respond? — If you were Mingzhe, how would you find a faithful way between your manager’s request and this good work?
lessons.jesus: Scripture describes Jesus as one “who went about doing good” (Acts 10:38). He washed his disciples’ feet, broke bread for hungry crowds, and cooked breakfast on the beach for tired fishermen. Most of his good works drew no applause, and his greatest good work was laying down his life for us on the cross. Every stitch we sew, we learned from him.
lessons.pray: Dear Lord, thank you for loving me with a lifetime of good works and finally with your own life. Use the ordinary tools in my hands to sew garment after garment into my colleagues’ everyday lives. When my efforts don’t count in my performance review, remind me that you see them all. And give me wisdom to walk faithfully between honouring my manager and continuing to do good. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Do one ‘refill the paper’ task today, unseen
Write down one useful tip and share it with a colleague
Prepare some practical help for someone in need at work
lessons.noon: “This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy” — Lord, right now let the work of my hands become a blessing to someone.

lessons.title: The Metal Detector
lessons.theme: True goodness abhors evil and clings to what is good

v: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light,
for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth,
proving what is well pleasing to the Lord.
Have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness, but rather even reprove them.

lessons.still: Stand in the doorway, straighten your back and plant your feet. Say to the Lord: “Lord, if anyone invites me down a dark path today, help me stand firm. I am a child of light, not of darkness.”
teach: Paul writes, “Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good” (Romans 12:9). Goodness is not being a pushover who says yes to everything. True goodness has discernment and a backbone: an almost instinctive revulsion at evil and an active pull towards what is good. Ephesians is even more concrete: “the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth,” and “Have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness” (Ephesians 5:9, 11). Goodness, righteousness and truth are fruit of the same tree.

At the end of a food factory’s production line there is a metal detector. It isn’t being fussy; it is protecting whoever will eat the food. Even a tiny broken needle tip must be caught. A good person carries a detector like that inside. Padded expense claims, under-the-table kickbacks, hiding a defect from a customer — people say, ‘That’s just how the industry works,’ but the Holy Spirit sets off a beep in your heart. That beep is not there to make you look superior; it protects you, protects your customers, and protects the name of God.

Refusing to go along with wrongdoing often has a cost: being called ‘not a team player’, being frozen out, even losing a promotion. But Paul reminds us that we “are now light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). This doesn’t mean becoming the office police, judging everyone. It means living as children of light: declining gently, explaining honestly, and when necessary raising concerns through proper channels. If you are asked to do something illegal, obey God rather than people (Acts 5:29), and seek help from someone you trust or a professional. You don’t have to carry it alone.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Bible is my standard, not ‘industry practice’. Saying no to wrongdoing is not proud self-righteousness; it is humbly returning to my place — letting God be God and letting his standard be King in my work, building God’s order.
lessons.scene: Sarah is a sales rep at a building-supplies company in Auckland. At month-end, a senior colleague slides a stack of receipts across her desk: “Just sign off these meals as your client entertainment. Everyone does it, and the boss knows.” She wasn’t at a single one of those dinners. Her colleague waits, the pen lying on top of the receipts.
q: Who is God? — Children of light bear fruit “in all goodness and righteousness and truth”. What does this tell you about the God who is light?
Who am I? — In your industry, what ‘everyone does it’ practices make your heart beep?
How shall I respond? — If you were Sarah, how would you answer your colleague both gently and clearly?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus saw traders and money-changers in the temple, he overturned their tables. He refused to compromise with the Pharisees’ hypocrisy, yet he was full of compassion for sinners who had fallen. His goodness had both an edge and warmth: he hates sin but loves sinners. In the wilderness he overcame temptation three times with the word of God, and opened a way of victory for us.
lessons.pray: Holy Lord, you are light, and in you there is no darkness at all. I confess that to fit in and avoid offending people, I sometimes turn a blind eye to small dishonesties. Keep the detector in my heart sensitive. Give me courage to say no gently and clearly, and wisdom to find a right way forward. Let me live at work as a child of light. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Check your expense claims or records are honest
When someone says ‘everyone does it’, pause and ask God
Prepare one sentence to gently refuse an improper request
lessons.noon: “Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good” — Lord, right now keep the detector in my heart sensitive.

lessons.title: Water, Not Fire
lessons.theme: Overcoming evil with good means handing the right to avenge back to God

v: Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honourable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.”
Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath and think of the person who wronged you. You don’t have to pretend it’s fine. Just say to the Lord: “Lord, vengeance belongs to you. I hand you this account, and I won’t carry it to work today.”
teach: Paul says, “Repay no one evil for evil,” and “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath” (Romans 12:17, 19). Quoting Proverbs, he says that if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if thirsty, give him a drink, “for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head” (Romans 12:20). This is not a cleverer form of revenge. It is unexpected goodness that sets the other person’s conscience burning. Then the summary: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).

Firefighters never fight fire with fire; they use water. Repaying evil with evil is like throwing another log on the blaze: the fire grows and eventually burns you too. Overcoming evil with good means answering with a different element, so the fire runs out of fuel. When we are set up at work, the natural reaction is to gather evidence and wait for a chance to hit back. The gospel invites us to use water, not fire. Joseph did exactly this. His brothers sold him into Egypt; years later they were at his mercy, and he comforted them with kind words.

Joseph said, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?” (Genesis 50:19). That question exposes the heart of pride: taking revenge is trying to sit in God’s judgement seat. Joseph stayed in his place and let God be God, and so he saw the bigger picture: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Overcoming evil with good doesn’t mean pretending the harm never happened or letting people walk all over you. When needed, you can still state the facts through proper channels and seek help from someone you trust. But your heart is no longer chained to revenge.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. “Am I in the place of God?” Laying down the right to avenge ourselves, returning to our place, and letting God be God — that is what an overcomer at work looks like.
lessons.scene: Liwei is a planner at an advertising agency in Shanghai. Last month a teammate presented Liwei’s idea as his own at a pitch, then blamed Liwei when something went wrong. Now that teammate’s project is stuck, the client wants to see it tomorrow, and the key consumer data sits only on Liwei’s laptop. A message arrives: “Could you help me out?” Liwei stares at it and doesn’t reply.
q: Who is God? — God says, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay.” What kind of judge does this show him to be?
Who am I? — Is there still an account in your heart that you want to ‘settle yourself’?
How shall I respond? — If you were Liwei, what reply would overcome evil with good while still being honest about what happened?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was betrayed, falsely accused and mocked, yet on the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He did not repay evil with evil, and he was not overcome by evil. Three days later he rose from the dead, overcoming the deepest evil with the greatest good. We can let go of revenge because he has already won this battle for us.
lessons.pray: Righteous Lord, you know the wrong I have suffered, and the account I want to settle. I confess I want to sit in your judgement seat. Today I hand the right to avenge back to you. Give me strength to answer my colleague with water, not fire, and wisdom to state the facts honestly when that is needed. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray one sentence of blessing over someone who hurt you
Don’t repeat anything today that would harm them
If needed, record the facts and give them to the right person
lessons.noon: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” — Lord, right now I hand the right to avenge back to you.

lessons.title: The Lighting Technician
lessons.theme: Do good in secret, because the Father sees in secret

v: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.

Therefore, when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does,
so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

lessons.still: Before you leave, quietly choose one good thing to do today that only you and God will know about. Say to the Lord: “Lord, this is my gift to you. No one else needs to see it. It is enough that you see.”
teach: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says, “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). Some people of his day gave as if sounding a trumpet ahead of themselves, wanting everyone to notice. Jesus said, “they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2). The applause was all they would get. Jesus points to another way: “don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does,” so that your good deeds are done in secret, “then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:3–4).

When the curtain falls on a great play, the audience applauds the actors, but few think of the lighting technician. All night they sat in the dark, timing every scene change, every fade up and fade out. Without them the stage would be black. Workplaces are full of lighting technicians: the one who quietly tidies the meeting notes, the one who switches off the machine a colleague forgot, the one who checks an extra detail for a client and never mentions it in the report. The Father has the best seat in the house. He can see backstage.

Jesus is not saying good deeds must never be seen. He also said, “let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father” (Matthew 5:16). The key is motive: am I doing this so people see me, or so they see God? Good deeds done from self-centredness end with my reputation; good deeds done from the self-emptied life end with God’s glory. When we no longer need to be seen, we are set free from the grip of human applause.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. Hidden good works are the best gym for practising the self-emptied life: not for myself, only for Jesus and for others. Change your thinking — from ‘people should know what I did’ to ‘it is enough that the Father knows’.
lessons.scene: Peijun is a civil servant at a district office in Taipei. Just before closing, an elderly woman who cannot read came in to apply for a benefit. Peijun stayed and helped her fill in the form box by box, leaving forty minutes late. On the MRT home she opens social media. She has already typed a post and attached a photo of the old woman from behind. Her finger hovers over ‘Post’.
q: Who is God? — “Your Father who sees in secret”: how does this show you the Father notices what no one else sees?
Who am I? — When you do something good, whose eyes do you care about most?
How shall I respond? — If you were Peijun, would you publish that post? Why or why not?
lessons.jesus: Jesus worked many miracles, yet often told those he healed not to spread the news. In the wilderness he refused the temptation to leap from the temple and win the crowd’s amazement. His greatest good deed — bearing the sin of the world on the cross — was done as darkness covered the land. The moment least seen was the moment of deepest love.
lessons.pray: Father who sees in secret, I confess that I often long to be seen, liked and affirmed. Thank you for seeing the efforts no one knows about, and for seeing the part of me that wants applause. Purify my motives, so that today’s good deeds are for you and for others, not for me. Your seeing is enough. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Do one small good thing only you and God know about
After doing good today, resist telling anyone
Specifically thank a colleague who serves quietly
lessons.noon: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” — Lord, right now I don’t need applause; it is enough that you see.

mem.t: Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

lessons.title: The Parcel Desk
lessons.theme: Everything in my hands is entrusted to me, not owned by me

v: So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants and stewards of God’s mysteries.
Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?

lessons.still: Take out your staff pass or your keys and hold them in your palm. Say to the Lord: “Lord, this position, this job, these resources are all things you have entrusted to me. Today let me be a faithful steward and give you a good account.”
teach: Paul writes, “So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants and stewards of God’s mysteries. Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:1–2). In the ancient world, a steward managed his master’s household. He held the keys and the ledgers, but owned none of it. What the master required was not brilliance or talent, but faithfulness. Jesus said the same: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). The real test of faithfulness is rarely the big things; it is the small things nobody is watching.

In many apartment blocks, the concierge signs for residents’ parcels every day. Those boxes are not his. One may hold a designer handbag, another a pack of toilet rolls. He can’t open them or borrow them, and he has to record whose each one is, when it arrived and when it was collected. A good concierge doesn’t toss a box aside because it’s small, or skip the log because nobody checks. At work, the company’s budget, our clients’ data and our team’s time are all parcels like that: they pass through our hands, but they don’t belong to us.

“If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?” (Luke 16:12). Here is a shift in perspective: from ‘this is mine’ to ‘this is entrusted to me by the Lord’. The self-centred person treats a position like a throne and resources like private property. The self-emptied person knows they are a steward and the Master is King. Once we understand that everything is entrusted, we won’t misuse it — and we needn’t be anxious either, because the one we will give account to is a Lord both loving and just.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus be King — I am the steward, not the owner. Humility is returning to the steward’s place: letting people be people and God be God. Being faithful in the smallest things is how, bit by bit, we build God’s order.
lessons.scene: Noah is a night-shift supervisor at a logistics warehouse in Wellington. At three in the morning the last load has been shelved. Company rules say twenty bin locations must be spot-checked before each shift ends. He is the only one left in the building; no manager will check and his team has gone home. He is exhausted. His finger is on the ‘Confirm complete’ button, but the spot-check sheet is still blank.
q: Who is God? — God entrusts his mysteries to human stewards. What does this show you about the trust and hopes he has for you?
Who am I? — In your work, what are really ‘other people’s parcels’ that you have been treating as your own?
How shall I respond? — If you were Noah, at three in the morning with no one watching, what would you do?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was the Father’s most faithful servant. He said, “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). All his life he faithfully carried out what the Father had entrusted to him, and on the cross he said, “It is finished!” (John 19:30). That was a faithful steward’s perfect account.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for entrusting this job, these resources and these people to me. I confess that sometimes I treat them as my own, and sometimes I cut corners when no one is looking. Remind me that I am the steward and you are the Master. In every small task today, help me work faithfully, so that I can give you my account with a clear conscience. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Finish properly one task ‘nobody will check’
Return one shared item or file to its proper place
Before leaving, spend a minute giving the Lord your account
lessons.noon: “It is required of stewards that they be found faithful” — Lord, right now I want to complete what is in my hands faithfully, for you.

lessons.title: The Dawn Delivery Van
lessons.theme: I can be faithful because God is faithful to me first

v: This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.
It is because of The LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
“The LORD is my portion,” says my soul. “Therefore I will hope in him.”
The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.
It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.

lessons.still: When you wake, don’t reach for your phone yet. Sit on the edge of the bed and say to the Lord: “Lord, your loving kindness is new again this morning. I don’t have to carry yesterday’s failure into today. I put my hope in you.” Then breathe in and out slowly three times.
teach: Lamentations is poetry written among ruins. Jerusalem had fallen, the temple was burned, and the poet felt trapped in darkness. Yet right at the centre of chapter 3 he says, “This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope” (Lamentations 3:21). What does he recall? “It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

Before dawn, a delivery van pulls up outside the convenience store and unloads rice balls, sandwiches and milk, right on time. Whether yesterday’s sales were good or bad, whether a typhoon has just passed or it’s the eve of the New Year, the van comes; the shelves are freshly stocked every morning. God’s loving kindness arrives on time like that. It doesn’t check yesterday’s figures or whether you prayed properly last night. You don’t have to live today on yesterday’s leftover grace; he has sent a fresh delivery.

This week is about faithfulness, but the first step is not gritting our teeth to become people who keep our word. It is lifting our eyes to the God who keeps his. “The LORD is my portion” (Lamentations 3:24). When he becomes my foundation, my faithfulness at work is no longer only about keeping my job or my reputation; it flows from his faithfulness. Life first, then living: only people gripped by God’s faithfulness can grow the fruit of faithfulness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on your circumstances. Redundancy, low seasons and rejection are temporary; God’s loving kindness is eternal. Turning from the earthly to the heavenly, and drawing fresh strength each morning, is where an overcomer begins.
lessons.scene: Youting was made redundant three months ago. At seven this morning she received her twelfth email beginning, “Thank you for your application. Unfortunately…”. She sits at the kitchen table looking at a CV she has rewritten again and again. She had planned to apply to five more companies today, but right now all she wants is to close the laptop and go back to bed for the whole day.
q: Who is God? — Among the ruins, the poet says, “Great is your faithfulness.” How does this help you know God’s faithfulness?
Who am I? — What failure or weariness from yesterday are you carrying into this morning?
How shall I respond? — If you were Youting, how could today begin afresh within God’s faithfulness?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the greatest proof of God’s faithfulness. God promised a Saviour, and after centuries he came. Jesus told his disciples he would rise on the third day, and he walked out of the tomb. He promised, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Every morning he is there; he never fails to turn up.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, your loving kindness is new every morning. Today I come to you tired and disappointed. Please take from me yesterday’s rejections, failures and self-doubt. As I look for work, wait for replies and do the small things in front of me, help me remember that you are my portion. Give me strength to take today’s one small step. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: First thing this morning, read Lamentations 3:22–23 aloud
Write down three ways God has led you faithfully at work
Send a word of encouragement to a friend who is struggling
lessons.noon: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” — Lord, right now I don’t look back at yesterday; I look to you.

lessons.title: When the Price of Steel Rises
lessons.theme: Faithfulness means my word stands, even when it costs me

v: LORD, who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?
He who walks blamelessly and does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart;
he who doesn’t slander with his tongue, nor does evil to his friend, nor casts slurs against his fellow man;
in whose eyes a vile man is despised, but who honours those who fear the LORD; he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change;
he who doesn’t lend out his money for usury, nor take a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be shaken.
But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.

lessons.still: Think of what you have promised someone today. Quietly say to the Lord: “Lord, let my words carry weight. When I say ‘Yes’, let it really be yes; when I say ‘No’, let it really be no.”
teach: Psalm 15 asks a big question: “LORD, who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?” (Psalm 15:1). The answer is not religious activity but a string of everyday character: walking blamelessly, speaking truth in the heart, not slandering, not taking bribes. One line cuts especially deep: “he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change” (Psalm 15:4). The person who draws near to God is someone whose word stands — even when circumstances change and conditions get worse.

Small-business owners know the feeling: the quote has gone out, and then the price of raw materials suddenly jumps. Nothing has been signed yet; it was only a verbal agreement. Changing the price seems perfectly reasonable. Quotes usually carry a ‘valid until’ date, but in the heart of a faithful person the quote is valid from the moment the words leave their mouth. Jesus said, “let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). In God’s kingdom, your verbal promise is a contract.

Faithfulness is not blind stubbornness, and it doesn’t rule out conversation. If you truly cannot deliver, you can explain honestly and negotiate humbly — but not invent excuses to back out, or quietly lower the quality behind the scenes. Keeping your word often costs a temporary loss; breaking it costs lasting trust. Profit on one order can be earned again; broken trust is very hard to repair. When we are willing to lose out in order to keep our word, God receives glory through us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Relationships matter more than things; don’t destroy a relationship for the sake of things. Taking a loss to keep your word is self-denial — for Jesus, for others, not for yourself. It shifts our gaze from temporary profit to eternal faithfulness.
lessons.scene: Cheng’en runs a small machining workshop in Taoyuan. Last month he verbally agreed to make a batch of parts at the old price for a customer of ten years. This week the price of steel jumped by nearly twenty per cent. At the agreed price, the order will make almost no profit. Nothing is signed, and his salesman suggests: “Just tell them the quote was a mistake and send a new one.” He picks up the phone to call the customer.
q: Who is God? — God delights in the one who “keeps an oath even when it hurts”. What does this show you about how God keeps his own covenant?
Who am I? — Is there a promise you’ve made recently that you want to take back because things have changed?
How shall I respond? — If you were Cheng’en, how would you make this call in a way that is both faithful and honest?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus faced the cup of the cross — the greatest ‘loss’ ever taken. He could have refused to drink it, yet he prayed, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He kept the covenant of salvation the Father had prepared for us, at the cost of his own life. We can stand before God today because he did not change.
lessons.pray: Covenant-keeping God, you never go back on your word; you did not even spare your own Son for me. I confess that when conditions change and my interests suffer, I want to find a reason to take back what I said. Give me courage to keep my promises and wisdom to communicate honestly. Let my ‘Yes’ be yes and my ‘No’ be no, so that customers and colleagues see your faithfulness in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List today’s promises to others and check each one
If you can’t keep an agreement, explain honestly first
Before saying ‘Yes’, ask yourself if you truly can
lessons.noon: “He who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change” — Lord, right now let the words I speak carry your faithfulness.

lessons.title: Trust on the Timetable
lessons.theme: Faithfulness lives in being on time, keeping appointments and delivering

v: “Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them.
He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.

lessons.still: Look at today’s calendar and read each appointment time to yourself. Say to the Lord: “Lord, these hours are not only mine; others have entrusted them to me. Today help me to be on time, keep my commitments and deliver when I said I would.”
teach: In the parable of the talents, Jesus says the master returned “after a long time” to settle accounts. The servant who had received five talents brought his results, and the master said, “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew 25:21). The master praised faithfulness — and faithfulness was built up slowly through the ‘long time’ when the master was away. Proverbs puts it like this: “As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him” (Proverbs 25:13).

People trust the high-speed rail not because of its advertising, but because when the timetable says it leaves at a certain time, it does. A punctuality record isn’t built in a day; it is kept train after train, day after day. Trust at work is built the same way: arriving at meetings on time, delivering on Friday when you said Friday, actually calling back when you promised. Added together, these small things become your timetable, and others can safely hand things over to you.

“The cold of snow in the time of harvest” — harvest was the hottest, busiest season, and a reliable person was like a cool breeze. In workplaces used to delay and excuses, a Christian who does what they say is a witness in themselves. But this doesn’t come from our own perfectionism; it comes from working before the Lord. Use your heart and lean on the Spirit: hand every commitment to God, ask him to help you order your time, and be honest about your limits, not promising what you can’t deliver.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Faithfulness is a fruit of the Spirit, and it is the most concrete form of 920 at work — every ‘2’ around me gets a small taste of Christ’s reliability through my punctuality and kept promises.
lessons.scene: Wei Jie is a freelance designer in Singapore juggling three projects. He promised a coffee brand its packaging design by noon on Friday. It is now eleven on Thursday night and he is only halfway through. A friend messages him: “Just say the file got corrupted and you have to redo it. Two extra days — no one will know.” He looks at the message, then at the unfinished design on his screen.
q: Who is God? — The master praises the “good and faithful servant”. What does this show you that God values?
Who am I? — How punctual is your ‘work timetable’? Where do you most often run late?
How shall I respond? — If you were Wei Jie, besides lying or pulling an all-nighter, what honest options are there?
lessons.jesus: Jesus lived his whole life according to the Father’s timing. When pressed, he said, “My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4). When the time came, “he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). He never ran away early and never dragged his feet. The salvation of the cross was delivered right on God’s schedule.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, you are never late and you never break an appointment. I confess that I often procrastinate and then cover it with excuses. Help me order my time well, arrive on time and deliver as promised; and when I truly can’t make it, give me courage to say so honestly and early. Let my reliability in small things be a cool breeze to colleagues and clients. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Arrive two minutes early to every meeting today
Set a clear delivery date for one delayed task
If you’ll miss a deadline, say so early, without excuses
lessons.noon: “You have been faithful over a few things” — Lord, right now let me be faithful in this small thing in front of me.

lessons.title: The Access Card
lessons.theme: A trusted person can open a door for God’s kingdom

v: Then this Daniel was distinguished above the presidents and the local governors, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.

Then the presidents and the local governors sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.
Then these men said, “We won’t find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.”
Joseph found favour in his sight. He ministered to him, and Potiphar made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. The LORD’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field.

lessons.still: Hold your access card or office key in your hand. Say to the Lord: “Lord, thank you that I am trusted here. Please use this trust as a door through which others can come to know you.”
teach: Daniel served as an official in a foreign court. His rivals hunted for something to accuse him of, “but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him” (Daniel 6:4). In the end they said, “We won’t find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God” (Daniel 6:5). Joseph was the same. Potiphar put “all that he had” into his hand, and “the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake” (Genesis 39:4–5). Their faithfulness let outsiders see God.

An access card is a piece of trust. A new hire can only get through the front door; a senior engineer can enter the server room; the person the boss trusts completely even knows the code to the safe. The deeper the trust, the more doors open. It is the same in God’s kingdom. When colleagues, managers and clients trust you, they come to you in their hardest moments and open the doors of their hearts as well. In that moment, your faithfulness becomes a doorway for God’s kingdom.

Daniel and Joseph were not trusted because they evangelised first; they were trusted first, and then their lives became a witness to God. Being trusted is not a reason to exalt ourselves but a way for Jesus to receive the glory. When someone rings you late at night simply because they trust you, God has opened a door. Guard their privacy carefully, and gently bring them to Jesus. This is how 235 begins: at work, becoming spiritual companions and spiritual family to one another.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Faithfulness earns trust, trust opens the door of relationship, and God works within the relationship. Building God’s order often begins with one trusted Christian.
lessons.scene: Guanlin is an associate director at an accounting firm in Taipei. At ten on Friday night his boss suddenly rings him, his voice hoarse. Something has happened at home; his wife is moving out, and he doesn’t know who to tell. “You’re the only person at the firm I trust.” Guanlin grips the phone. He wants to ask, “Could I pray for you?” but is afraid of overstepping.
q: Who is God? — Through Daniel’s and Joseph’s faithfulness, outsiders saw God. How does this God use the faithfulness of ordinary people?
Who am I? — At work, who has handed you their ‘access card’?
How shall I respond? — If you were Guanlin, how would you respond to this call so that you respect boundaries and still bring your boss to Jesus?
lessons.jesus: Revelation calls the rider on the white horse “Faithful and True” (Revelation 19:11). Jesus never breaks faith, and he revealed the Father’s heart completely. The Samaritan woman, Nicodemus, Zacchaeus — because they could trust him, they opened the deepest doors of their hearts to him. Today he wants to use your faithfulness to lead people through the door of the kingdom.
lessons.pray: Faithful and True Lord, thank you that people trust me at work. Keep me from becoming proud because of it, and from betraying that trust. When someone opens their heart to me, give me careful lips, a gentle heart and fitting words. Help me keep good boundaries without missing the doors you open. May my faithfulness become a doorway for others to know you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Keep a colleague’s private matter to yourself
Do one entrusted task so well others can relax
Pray for someone who trusts you, that God opens their heart
lessons.noon: “Because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him” — Lord, right now let my faithfulness be a witness to you.

mem.t: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.title: The Fader on the Mixing Desk
lessons.theme: A gentle answer can bring a blaze of anger down

v: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.
The men of Ephraim said to him, “Why have you treated us this way, that you didn’t call us when you went to fight with Midian?” They rebuked him sharply.
He said to them, “What have I now done in comparison with you? Isn’t the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?
God has delivered into your hand the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb! What was I able to do in comparison with you?” Then their anger was abated towards him when he had said that.

lessons.still: Relax your shoulders, lower your chin a little, and say this once in a voice slightly softer than usual: “Lord, give me a gentle tongue today. When others get loud, let me get quiet; when others are rushed, let me be steady.”
teach: Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1), and “A gentle tongue is a tree of life” (Proverbs 15:4). Judges gives us a living example. Gideon had just won a victory, but the men of Ephraim came to confront him for not calling them to the fight: “They rebuked him sharply” (Judges 8:1). Gideon didn’t argue.
