Instead he honoured their achievement: “What was I able to do in comparison with you?” And “their anger was abated towards him when he had said that” (Judges 8:3).

Every sound engineer knows that when one channel starts to distort at a live event, the worst thing you can do is push the other faders up to drown it out. The right move is to bring the fader slowly down. Conflict works the same way. When the other person’s volume rises, our instinct is to push ours up too, and soon the whole room is screeching with feedback. A gentle answer pulls the fader down: lower the volume, slow the pace, respond to the emotion first and the issue second.

Gideon could be gentle because he didn’t need the credit. He had won the battle, yet he handed the honour to others, and that takes a heart not centred on itself. Harsh words usually come from self-centredness: I must win, I must be seen, I can’t lose out. Gentleness is not weakness; it is strength choosing restraint. A seasoned sound engineer isn’t unable to push the volume up — they simply know when to bring it down. This is fruit of the Spirit, not merely a communication technique.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility draws out humility and both sides win; pride provokes pride and both sides lose. By giving away the credit, Gideon gave away a path to peace. Use your heart and lean on the Spirit, not your head and your own strength — when anger rushes in, turn your focus to Jesus first.
lessons.scene: Shufen works at a cosmetics counter in a department store in Kaohsiung. On Saturday afternoon, at the busiest hour, a customer brings back a half-used bottle of skincare and loudly declares she has been cheated. A small crowd gathers. Company policy says opened products can’t be refunded. Shufen feels wronged too, and “Madam, rules are rules” is already on the tip of her tongue.
q: Who is God? — God says, “A gentle tongue is a tree of life.” What does this show you about how much he cares about the way we speak?
Who am I? — When someone raises their voice at you, does your ‘fader’ usually go up or come down?
How shall I respond? — If you were Shufen, how could you keep company policy and still answer this customer gently?
lessons.jesus: On the night Jesus was arrested, one of those with him drew a sword and cut off the right ear of the high priest’s servant. Jesus said, “Let me at least do this” — and he touched his ear and healed him (Luke 22:51). At the most explosive moment, he did not push the volume up; he answered hostility with healing.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives peace, you know my temper, and you know the fire inside me when people shout at me. Rule my tongue today. When customers, colleagues or managers get worked up, help me lower my voice first and turn my heart to you. Give me wisdom to hold to what is right and still answer with gentle words, so that anger stops with me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When someone raises their voice, deliberately lower yours
Before responding to a complaint, say “I can see you’re worried”
Give a colleague credit for their work
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath” — Lord, right now let me lower my voice and turn my heart to you.

lessons.title: No Rush to Post the Screenshots
lessons.theme: The gentle entrust their reputation to God

v: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married; for he had married a Cushite woman.
They said, “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” And the LORD heard it.
Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.
The LORD spoke suddenly to Moses, to Aaron, and to Miriam, “You three come out to the Tent of Meeting!” The three of them came out.
The LORD came down in a pillar of cloud, and stood at the door of the Tent, and called Aaron and Miriam; and they both came forward.
He said, “Now hear my words. If there is a prophet amongst you, I, the LORD, will make myself known to him in a vision. I will speak with him in a dream.
My servant Moses is not so. He is faithful in all my house.
With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see the LORD’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”

lessons.still: Remember the last time you were misunderstood, but don’t replay it again. Fold your hands and say to the Lord: “Lord, my reputation is in your hands. Today I won’t rush to defend myself. I will be still before you first.”
teach: Miriam and Aaron were Moses’ sister and brother, and his closest co-workers. They criticised him over the Cushite woman he had married, then revealed their real grievance: “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” (Numbers 12:2). Scripture then adds a note: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth” (Numbers 12:3). Notice that the text records no reply from Moses. It simply says, “And the LORD heard it,” and then God himself steps in to speak for him.

Many workplaces today have a ‘screenshot defence’ culture. The moment we are misunderstood, we rush to post chat logs in the group, lay out a timeline and tag everyone involved. Sometimes stating the facts is necessary. But often the urgency behind it is fear for our image. Moses’ humility wasn’t a lack of feeling; it was not rushing to defend himself. He knew that God was the one who would ultimately speak for him.

God said of Moses, “He is faithful in all my house” (Numbers 12:7). Moses’ gentleness had roots: his security did not come from his colleagues’ approval but from speaking with God face to face. Gentle people are not spineless; they place their reputation in God’s hands. When Miriam was later struck with leprosy, Moses cried out to God to heal her (Numbers 12:13). This is the self-emptied life: not fighting for oneself, but praying for those who have hurt us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying power down, returning to our place, and letting God be God. Not rushing to clear our name leaves the judgement seat to God. Use your heart and lean on the Spirit, rather than your head to plot a counter-attack.
lessons.scene: Haitao is an operations manager at an e-commerce company in Shenzhen, promoted from the front line only last year. This week he heard that two senior colleagues have been saying he ‘got promoted through connections’, and have complained to the director that his rotas are unfair. His phone holds every rota and every message. He is about to compile a long explanation and post it in the department group.
q: Who is God? — “And the LORD heard it”: what does this show you about how God cares for those who are slandered?
Who am I? — When you are misunderstood, what are you most anxious to protect?
How shall I respond? — If you were Haitao, what explanation is necessary, and what reaction would come from self-centredness?
lessons.jesus: Before Pilate, Jesus was falsely accused by many, yet “He gave him no answer, not even one word” (Matthew 27:14). It wasn’t that he had nothing to say; he entrusted himself to the Father. Three days later the Father raised him from the dead — the greatest vindication of all. We too can safely place our reputation in this Father’s hands.
lessons.pray: Father, you have heard what people are saying about me, and you see the hurt and resentment in my heart. I so want to lay out all the evidence right now and prove I’m right. Help me first be still before you, and discern which explanations are necessary and which reactions come from self-centredness. And give me strength to bless those two colleagues. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When misunderstood, pray first, reply second
State only necessary facts, without emotional adjectives
Speak one blessing to God for someone who criticised you
lessons.noon: “Now the man Moses was very humble” — Lord, right now I place my reputation in your hands.

lessons.title: The Instructor’s Brake
lessons.theme: Take Jesus’ yoke and learn his gentle and humble ways

v: “Come to me, all you who labour and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps,
who didn’t sin, “neither was deceit found in his mouth.”
When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.

lessons.still: Put down the bag on your shoulder and picture laying today’s burdens at the Lord’s feet. Say to him: “Lord, I am weary and heavily burdened. I come to you. Please give me rest, and teach me to learn from you.”
teach: Jesus said, “Come to me, all you who labour and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” Then: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:28–29). In the Gospels Jesus rarely describes his own heart so directly, and the words he chooses are “gentle and humble”. A yoke was the wooden frame laid across the necks of two oxen so they could pull the plough together. Jesus invites us to share a yoke with him and let him lead.

In a driving-school car, there is a second brake pedal under the passenger seat. Learner drivers inevitably get flustered, and a good instructor doesn’t shout at them. He sits calmly and, when needed, presses the brake gently to slow the car. Jesus’ yoke is like that. He sits in the car with us; he doesn’t frighten us with rebukes until we are even more tense, but teaches us his rhythm through his gentle presence. People who have been taught like that are the ones who know how to teach others gently.

Peter writes that Christ left “you an example, that you should follow his steps”; “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:21, 23). His gentleness was not weakness; it was all power choosing to entrust itself to the Father. When we are worn out and short-tempered at work, what we need most is not more self-control but to come back to him, take his yoke, and let his gentleness flow into us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example; the Holy Spirit is my guide. Gentleness isn’t squeezed out by willpower; it comes from taking his yoke and learning from him. Use your heart and you’ll find joy; use only your head and you’ll find worry. Rest in him first, and you will have the strength to be gentle with others.
lessons.scene: Xiaolei is the emergency-department nurse manager at a hospital in Chengdu. She has worked six night shifts in a row, and the unit is badly understaffed. At four in the morning, a newly graduated nurse comes to ask, for the third time, how to set the same infusion pump. Xiaolei feels anger surge up; her voice is already sharper than usual. She also knows that if this goes on, she won’t be able to hold out much longer.
q: Who is God? — Jesus says he is “gentle and humble in heart”. How does this change the way you see him?
Who am I? — What burdens are you carrying at work that are wearing your patience thin?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiaolei, how could she answer the new nurse right now — and how should she look after herself?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had authority to still storms and drive out demons, yet he chose to ride into Jerusalem on a young donkey. He took children in his arms, touched lepers, and waited at a well for a woman others looked down on. This gentle and humble Lord still says to every exhausted worker: come to me.
lessons.pray: Gentle and humble Lord, I am truly tired — so tired that even my words to the people around me have thorns. I lay my burdens at your feet; please give me rest. Teach me to take your yoke and learn from you, so that even in the most pressured moments I can be gentle. Give me courage, too, to tell my managers about the staffing problems, and to seek help from someone I trust when I need it. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before answering a question, breathe once and slow down
Report understaffing or overwork honestly to your manager
Take five quiet minutes today to lay burdens before God
lessons.noon: “I am gentle and humble in heart” — Lord, right now I put down my burden and learn your gentleness.

lessons.title: The Bone-Setter’s Touch
lessons.theme: We correct people to restore them, not to prove ourselves right

v: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,

lessons.still: Think about whom you need to give feedback to today, and hand that person to the Lord: “Lord, I don’t want to beat them; I want to help them. Give me a gentle heart, and help me remember that I can fall too.”
teach: Paul writes, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1). The word ‘restore’ is used elsewhere in the New Testament for fishermen “mending their nets” (Matthew 4:21), and some commentators note it could describe setting a dislocated bone. Paul also reminds Timothy, “The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all,” “in gentleness correcting those who oppose him” (2 Timothy 2:24–25).

A good bone-setter’s hands are both steady and light. He doesn’t yank a misaligned bone so hard that the patient’s pain doubles. He calms them, finds exactly the right position, then uses just enough force to ease the bone back into place. Feedback at work is the same. When a team member or colleague makes a mistake, the goal is not to use the heaviest words to show how bad it was, but accurate, specific, just-enough pressure that helps them back into the right place and onto their feet.

Paul adds: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” The root of gentleness is humility: I know I can get things wrong too, and I have been gently restored by others. Proud correction is about proving I’m better than you; humble correction is about your good. Paul says, “Perhaps God may give them repentance” (2 Timothy 2:25). It is God who truly changes people, not the volume of our voice. Our responsibility is to speak the truth, and to speak it gently.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; don’t wound a person over a task. Correction aims at restoration, not at winning. Life first, then relationships: those who have been gently restored by the Lord are the ones who know how to restore others gently.
lessons.scene: Ravi is a tech lead at a software company in Kuala Lumpur. Reviewing a new engineer’s code today, he found a serious vulnerability that could leak customer data. In the review comment box he has already typed: “Even an intern wouldn’t make this mistake.” The cursor blinks. He hasn’t pressed Submit.
q: Who is God? — Paul says, “Perhaps God may give them repentance.” What does this show you about who really changes people?
Who am I? — When you give feedback, are you more like a bone-setter, or someone proving they are stronger?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ravi, how would you rewrite that review comment so it makes the seriousness clear and still carries gentleness?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus met the Samaritan woman, he didn’t open by exposing her wounds; he asked her for a drink. As they talked, he gently and clearly named the truth about her life, and revealed himself as the Christ. She wasn’t crushed by shame; she ran back into town and invited everyone to come and see him (John 4). Jesus’ correction always leads people towards life.
lessons.pray: Gentle Lord, you restored me so gently, never using my failures to humiliate me. Today, when I need to point out someone else’s mistakes, help me remember that I can fall too. Give me a bone-setter’s touch: accurate, specific and full of compassion. Let my feedback help people stand up rather than crushing them. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When giving feedback, begin with something done well
Address the problem, not the person
Afterwards, ask: “How can I help you with this?”
lessons.noon: “Restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” — Lord, right now let my feedback carry your gentleness.

lessons.title: Thirty Seconds to Undo
lessons.theme: Swift to hear, slow to speak — and let our writing be gentle too

v: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.

lessons.still: Before you open your inbox, take your hands off the keyboard and rest them on your chest. Say to the Lord: “Lord, every word I type today is before you. Make me swift to hear and slow to speak.”
teach: James writes, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:19–20). Paul adds, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). In James’s and Paul’s day, a letter had to be carried by hand for days before it arrived. Today an email or message lands the instant we press Send, and it can never be taken back.

Many email apps have a ‘schedule send’ or ‘undo send’ feature that gives you a few seconds to change your mind. That small design choice is surprisingly biblical: before sending, leave a gap for the Holy Spirit to speak. An angry reply written at eleven at night, reread the next morning, often makes us grateful we never sent it. In the world of writing, being ‘slow to speak’ means setting yourself a delay before you send.

This week has been about gentleness: the gentle answer, Moses’ humility, Jesus’ yoke, gentle correction. Today we bring it to our fingertips. Written words lack facial expression and tone, so they often wound more easily than spoken ones. Before sending, ask three questions: Is it true? Will it build others up? Am I letting Jesus be King, or letting my anger rule? The anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God; gentle words are what serve God’s purposes.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use your heart and lean on the Spirit, not your head and your own strength. Pausing before you send is handing control back to Jesus. Every recipient is one of my ‘2’; gentle writing is 920 bearing fruit on a screen.
lessons.scene: Aroha manages a travel agency in Christchurch. At eleven at night she receives an email from a partner hotel blaming her agency entirely for an overbooking, in a cutting tone, with her boss copied in. She immediately types a long reply, every line barbed, even dragging up the hotel’s last mistake. Her cursor rests on Send.
q: Who is God? — “The anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God”: how, then, is God’s righteousness worked out?
Who am I? — Where do you most often lose gentleness in writing: email, group chats, comments or private messages?
How shall I respond? — If you were Aroha, how could she handle this email so the facts are clear but anger isn’t in the driving seat?
lessons.jesus: John writes, “The Word became flesh and lived amongst us… full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). God’s most important word was not an angry letter dropped from heaven; he came in a human body to speak it in person. Jesus always spoke truth without losing grace. He is the gentlest letter God ever wrote to the world.
lessons.pray: Lord full of grace and truth, I confess I often lose my gentleness in front of a screen, and press Send wanting only to show how angry I am. When I am typing, remind me to stop and listen to you first. Let my words tell the truth and carry grace, make the facts clear and still build others up. In every email and message today, be King. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Wait at least ten minutes before answering an emotional email
Before sending, delete one aggressive adjective
Send one message today purely to build someone up
lessons.noon: “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” — Lord, right now let me listen to you before I press Send.

mem.t: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.

lessons.title: Able to Brake
lessons.theme: Ruling your own spirit is greater than taking a city

v: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.
Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.

lessons.still: Before you leave, place a hand on your chest. Breathe in slowly, breathe out slowly. Say to the Lord: “Lord, if someone presses on a sore spot today, hold my heart still first, and only then let me speak.”
teach: In the ancient world, taking a city was a warrior’s highest glory: it took courage, troops and strategy. Solomon turns the scales over: “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city” (Prov. 16:32). However high a city’s walls, they fall one day; the heart within is the hardest city a person will ever conquer. Elsewhere he says, “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint” (Prov. 25:28). A city without walls lets anyone in; a heart without self-control can lose a whole day’s peace to one remark or one email.

A good car depends not only on its accelerator but on its brakes. All the horsepower in the world is a danger, not a gift, if it cannot stop. Work is the same. Skill, eloquence and drive are the accelerator; self-control is the brake. Many careers are not lost through a lack of speed but through one meeting where the brakes failed: a heated word, a fist on the table, a reply sent at midnight that punched a hole in years of trust. Brakes do not stop you moving forward. They keep you safe on the bends.

Where does anger usually come from? Very often, from “I want to be in charge” being blocked: plans disrupted, face lost, people not doing it my way. That is the root of self-centredness. Self-control is not gritting your teeth; it is fruit the Spirit grows (Gal. 5:23). When I hand the throne to Jesus, I no longer need to fight every battle for myself. When I am wronged, I can return to my proper place: I am human, he is God, and justice is in his hands.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself. In anger the mind races to calculate who is winning; leaning on the Spirit, the heart grows quiet first. Humility means laying down power and returning to my place. I do not need to win every argument, because Jesus is King.
lessons.scene: Guanting is site manager on a housing development in Hsinchu. The subcontractor has failed to turn up for the third time, and the whole schedule slips again. In the project group chat he has typed a long, blazing message that names the subcontractor’s boss as well. His thumb hovers over “Send”. Thirty people will read it.
q: Who is God? — God is “slow to anger”. What security does his patience with you give you?
Who am I? — In what situations do your brakes most often fail? What are you trying to protect in that moment?
How shall I respond? — If you were Guanting, what would you do before pressing Send?
lessons.jesus: On the night Jesus was betrayed and bound, Peter drew a sword to defend him, but Jesus said, “Put your sword back into its place” (Matt. 26:52). He could have asked the Father for legions of angels, yet he chose not to strike back. “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Pet. 2:23). The greatest power is to be able to retaliate and to entrust yourself to God instead.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the one who could hold back your anger. I confess that I often flare up over lost face and disrupted plans, and I have hurt colleagues around me. Today, when I want to win an argument, hold my tongue and my fingers. Let me pause, pray, and only then respond. Reign in my heart and rule my spirit. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When anger rises, count to ten before speaking
Save any heated message as a draft; reread it in an hour
Apologise to one colleague I have snapped at
lessons.noon: “one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city” — Lord, right now I hand you this anger. Rule my spirit.

lessons.title: Small Rudder, Wildfire
lessons.theme: The tongue is small, yet it steers the whole ship

v: For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.
Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body.
Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.
So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity amongst our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind;
but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

lessons.still: Before work, gently close your mouth and press the tip of your tongue to the roof of your mouth for three seconds. Remind yourself: “Lord, my tongue is yours today. Before I speak, speak first in my heart.”
teach: James gives us three pictures in a row: the bit in a horse’s mouth, the small rudder on a great ship, and the small fire that sets a forest alight. Each is tiny; each changes everything. He admits candidly, “Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person” (Jas 3:2), and adds, “nobody can tame the tongue” (Jas 3:8). Most piercing of all is verse 9: the same mouth that praises God in a hymn in the morning curses “men who are made in the image of God” by the coffee machine at lunch. “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so” (Jas 3:10).

In today’s office the tongue does not live only in the mouth; it lives on the keyboard too. A sneer in the group chat, a barbed comment in a meeting, a screenshot forwarded on: like a cigarette end dropped in dry grass, nothing happens at first, and three days later the whole department is smouldering. The reverse is also true. A sincere “Thanks for covering for me” can act like a rudder and turn a colleague who was about to resign back on course. Every sentence you speak is steering somebody’s day.

When James says no one can tame the tongue, he is not calling us to despair but to surrender. The tongue’s problem is rooted in the self-centred heart: wanting to look right, wanting people to know I am not to be messed with, wanting to buy applause with a clever joke. When Christ lives in me, my words are no longer for me but for building others up. Taming the tongue begins with handing my mouth to the Lord each day.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Never wound a person just to win a point. The practice of 920 starts with the tongue: every word to the people around me (my “2”) can grow or strip away a fruit of the Spirit.
lessons.scene: Xinyi is an account manager at an advertising agency in Kuala Lumpur. A colleague’s pitch has been rejected by the client again, and in a private group chat everyone starts mocking him. Someone writes: “Xinyi, you’re the funny one. Finish him off.” She already has a line in mind, very funny and very cruel, blinking in the text box.
q: Who is God? — God created the world by his word, and his words bring life. How does that change the way you think about speaking?
Who am I? — Where does your tongue most often start fires: meetings, group chats, or complaining after work?
How shall I respond? — How could Xinyi avoid being a killjoy without delivering that final blow?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the Word made flesh, and gracious words came from his mouth. He rebuked hypocrisy, yet he never humiliated the weak for the pleasure of a sharp remark. To the woman caught in adultery he simply said, “Neither do I condemn you.” On the cross, his tongue was still praying for forgiveness for those who crucified him.
lessons.pray: Lord, you speak the word of life. I confess that my tongue often runs ahead of my heart; sometimes for a laugh, sometimes to vent, I have hurt people you love. Today, set a guard over my mouth in group chats, in meetings and on the phone. Let me speak words that build up. Let only blessing, not cursing, come from my mouth. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before posting in a chat, ask: does this build up?
Forward no screenshots or stickers mocking a colleague
Praise one colleague specifically for good work
lessons.noon: “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing.” — Lord, right now cleanse my mouth, and let only blessing go out from it.

lessons.title: The Exit Is Right There
lessons.theme: God is faithful; in temptation he provides a way out

v: Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall.

No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.

lessons.still: Before you sit down to work, open your hands as if setting something down. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you already know the temptations I will meet today. Let me see the way out you have made, and give me strength to turn.”
teach: Paul was writing to believers in Corinth, a busy port city full of commerce and full of temptation. First he warns: “let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall” (1 Cor. 10:12). Then comes a great promise: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape” (1 Cor. 10:13). To young Timothy he is blunter still: “Flee from youthful lusts” (2 Tim. 2:22). With some temptations, spiritual courage does not mean staying to test your willpower. It means turning round and walking away.

Every floor of an office building has green emergency exit signs. Nobody notices them on an ordinary day, but in a fire they save lives. The way out God provides is often right beside you: a reason to leave the dinner early, an arrangement not to share a car alone, a decision to put the phone in another room, a spiritual companion you can message. Workplace temptations come in many forms: kickbacks, flirtations, drinking-heavy client dinners, a report that would look better with one number changed, a late night alone with a browser. The sign will not walk for you, but it stays lit, pointing the way.

Desire is not all bad; God made us with longings. The trouble is the self-centred heart that wants to be in charge: I want it, and I want it now. Self-control means letting Jesus sit in the driving seat of my desires. Boundaries are not chains but protection; those who draw the line in advance do not have to wrestle in the moment. If you are already caught in something, do not struggle alone. Find a trusted spiritual companion and, where needed, seek professional help.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard and the Spirit is my guide. Change the mindset first: a boundary is not a loss but God’s protection. In 235, a spiritual companion is often the very “way of escape” God uses, and the self-emptied are willing to be seen and reminded.
lessons.scene: Yongfu is head of purchasing at a firm in Penang. A new supplier takes him to dinner, and during the meal slides a thick envelope across the table: “A small token. Please look after us with next quarter’s order.” Everyone else at the table smiles and pretends not to notice. Yongfu’s hand is resting on the table; his heart is pounding.
q: Who is God? — “God is faithful.” When have you realised, looking back, that he had in fact provided a way out?
Who am I? — At what times and in what settings are you most likely to let your guard down?
How shall I respond? — What could Yongfu say and do right now to take the way God has opened?
lessons.jesus: Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness, and the devil tempted him three times: with bread, with fame, and with the glory of the kingdoms. Each time he answered, “It is written.” He was “in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin”, so he can sympathise with my weakness and help me stand.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, thank you that you will not let me be tempted beyond what I can bear. I confess there are weak moments for me: at dinners, late at night, in front of a screen no one else sees. Open my eyes today to the way out you have prepared, and give me courage to turn. I want Jesus to be King over my desires. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the setting and time I most often stumble
Set one concrete boundary for that setting in advance
Message a spiritual companion and ask for prayer
lessons.noon: “will with the temptation also make the way of escape” — Lord, right now show me that way, and give me strength to take it.

lessons.title: The Stolen Fifteen Minutes
lessons.theme: Redeem the time and hand it back to the Lord

v: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore, don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

lessons.still: Before you go into work, put your phone face down on the desk and pause for thirty seconds. Say to the Lord: “Lord, every hour today is on loan from you. Teach me to count my days, and don’t let my attention be stolen.”
teach: Paul writes, “watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:15–16). “Redeeming” carries the sense of buying back, like a trader snapping up good stock in the market before anyone else. Moses, who saw in the wilderness how brief life is, prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (Ps. 90:12). Time is the asset God gives his stewards most evenly, and the one we waste most easily.

Many people go home exhausted yet unable to say what they achieved today. Open the screen-time report on your phone and the answer is often there: fifteen minutes of scrolling, seven times a day. Attention is like the air conditioning in an office. If the door is left open, the cool air keeps leaking out; you still pay the bill, but the room never cools down. Self-control with your phone is not about becoming an ascetic. It is about shutting the door, so that focus stays where it belongs: on the work in front of you, the people beside you, and the Lord within you.

Often we scroll not because we need to but because we are escaping: from a hard report, from the anxiety of empty space, from facing God in solitude. The self-centred try to fill themselves with stimulation; the self-emptied learn to be still in the Lord. “Understand what the will of the Lord is” (Eph. 5:17). Redeeming the time means letting Jesus be King over my calendar and my attention.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on yourself, others or your circumstances. The phone constantly pulls our focus to other people’s updates and the world’s noise. Shift perspective from the temporary to the eternal: these fifteen minutes can be invested in what lasts for ever.
lessons.scene: Yuxuan is a software engineer at a fintech company in Singapore. With the quarterly release looming, she is stuck on a stubborn bug. An hour has gone, and she notices she has opened a short-video app for the fifth time. Her manager messages: “How’s it going?” She stares at the screen and suddenly feels very empty.
q: Who is God? — God is the eternal God, and time is in his hands. How does that change how you see your day?
Who am I? — What do you most often use your phone to escape: pressure, boredom or loneliness?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yuxuan, how would you start the next hour afresh?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ public ministry lasted little more than three years, yet he was never in a hurry. When the crowds pressed in, “he withdrew himself into the desert and prayed”. When others pushed him, he said, “My time has not yet come.” He was not driven by others’ expectations, because he lived by the Father’s timetable. At the end he could say, “I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.”
lessons.pray: Lord of time, I confess that bit by bit I hand the time you give me over to a screen. Teach me to count my days and gain a heart of wisdom. Today, when I want to escape, remind me to come back to you and give myself fully to the task in front of me. Be King over my calendar and my attention. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Put my phone in a drawer for one hour of focused work
Delete or hide the app that steals most of my time
Spend ten minutes before bed praying, not scrolling
lessons.noon: “redeeming the time, because the days are evil” — Lord, right now I put down my phone and give this hour back to you.

lessons.title: The Nine-Fruit Radar
lessons.theme: Review growth in the servant life: count grace, face the truth

v: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

lessons.still: Before work today, pause for one extra minute. Look back quietly over these months and say: “Lord, thank you for walking with me all this way. Today I am not here to judge how good or bad I am, but to see what you have done in me.”
teach: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Gal. 5:22–23). Paul speaks of fruit, not output; it is grown, not manufactured. He also gives us a firm hope: “he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 1:6). In this stage we have travelled from servant leadership, humility, self-denial and faithfulness all the way through the nine fruits of the Spirit. Today we stop to see how the tree is growing.

Many companies hold annual performance reviews, but today is not an appraisal. It is more like the radar chart on a health check: nine points, each with its own score. The shape need not be perfectly symmetrical, but it honestly shows where you are full and where you are dented. Perhaps faithfulness is already high while gentleness is still sunken; perhaps joy is gradually returning while self-control keeps slipping. Seeing the dents is not condemnation. It shows you where the Spirit wants to work next.

Among the eight steps of a changed mindset (information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, multiplication), review and correction are the ones we often skip, yet they stop our practice from being a passing burst of enthusiasm. Ask honestly: what has changed in my mindset, my life, my lifestyle, my relationships and my ministry? Choose one area where you most want the Spirit to bear fruit, and set one correction. Please also open the app and complete the Workplace Health Self-Assessment, so that this review leaves a concrete record. Success is not proof; failure is not condemnation; Jesus is our focus.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Five changes from the inside out: mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships, ministry. In 920, the “9” is the fruit the Spirit grows, the “0” is the self-emptied life, and the “2” is every person around me. The aim of review is to let Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.scene: Qiuyue is a senior primary-school teacher in Taichung and leads her year group. She joined this course mid-term. Tonight, after marking homework, she takes out a notebook and draws her nine-fruit radar: patience and faithfulness reach far out, but gentleness and joy almost touch the centre. She remembers the harsh tone she used with a new teacher last week, and her pen stops.
q: Who is God? — Looking back on this stage, where has God shown you that “he will complete it”?
Who am I? — On your nine-fruit radar, which fruit is fullest, and which is most dented?
How shall I respond? — What concrete correction will you set for the next stage? Like Qiuyue, is there someone you need to go and speak to first?
lessons.jesus: The nine fruits are not a to-do list; they are a portrait of Jesus. His love went to the cross; his joy outlasted suffering; his gentleness lifted the bruised reed; his self-control kept him from calling down angels as he was nailed. The secret of fruitfulness is to remain in him, and let his life flow out through me.
lessons.pray: Lord who completes the good work, thank you for tending my heart these past months. Some fruit is beginning to grow, and I give you the glory. Some places are still hard and dry, and I will no longer pretend. Work in the dented places, so that at the office and at home I look more like Jesus. I place the next stage in your hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Draw my nine-fruit radar; mark the highest and lowest
Complete the Workplace Health Self-Assessment in the app
Write one line of testimony to grace; share it
lessons.noon: “he who began a good work in you will complete it” — Lord, right now I believe you are still at work in me.
